paragraphs.text: This report presents the findings of a survey of gas-side fouling in industrial heat-transfer equipment. The information came from personal contacts, visits to selected industries, attendance at professional meetings and conferences, and the open literature. Gas-side fouling and corrosion turn up in every energy-intensive industry, among them the chemical, petroleum, primary metals, pulp and paper, glass, cement, foodstuffs and textile industries. Six topics receive the main attention: (1) heat exchanger design procedures for gas-side fouling service, (2) the gas-side fouling factors currently available, (3) startup and shutdown procedures that limit fouling effects, (4) techniques for preventing, mitigating and accommodating gas-side fouling, (5) the economic impact of fouling on capital costs, maintenance costs, loss of production and energy losses, and (6) miscellaneous related considerations. The report sums up the state of the art for industrial gas-side fouling with a list of recommendations for further work.

Fouling of heat-transfer equipment has troubled energy-related industries for a long time. Most early work dealt with liquid-side fouling, but growing interest in recovering heat from exhaust gas streams, driven largely by rising fuel costs, has recently shifted much attention to gas-side fouling. The subject concerns private industry, public utilities, research organizations, national laboratories, professional societies, and local, state and federal government. To show the size and scope of the problem, the authors briefly review the main gas-side fouling activities of the previous 10-12 years.

Early milestones: in 1970 Battelle Columbus Laboratories, sponsored by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Research Committee on Corrosion and Deposits from Combustion Gases, issued an extensive bibliography on corrosion and deposits from combustion gases (Reference 1-1). In 1971 W. T. Reid published the now classic work on deposits and corrosion in boilers and gas turbines (Reference 1-2), and Taborek et al. (Reference 1-3) gave a systematic treatment of fouling that is regarded as a major contribution. In 1974 the same ASME committee, led by E. C. Winegartner, issued guidelines for coal fouling and slagging parameters (Reference 1-4). R. W. Bryers of the Foster Wheeler Development Corporation organized important international conferences on ash deposits and corrosion from combustion gases in 1978 and 1981 (Reference 1-5,6). At the Sixth International Heat Transfer Conference in Toronto in 1978, Epstein (Reference 1-7) proposed six basic types of fouling, a scheme that has since gained wide acceptance.

Later activities: Somerscales and Knudsen organized the first International Fouling Conference at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York, in 1979; its proceedings, published the next year, contain several strong review articles and a number of fouling R&D recommendations (Reference 1-8). In 1980 Battelle Columbus Laboratories finished a broad review of fireside additives for the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) (Reference 1-9), and the same year a workshop on oil and gas additives in Boston drew 116 representatives from industry, national laboratories and the electric utilities (Reference 1-10). In 1981 DOE sponsored the Workshop on the Assessment of Gas-Side Fouling in Fossil Fuel Exhaust Environments in Boulder, Colorado (Reference 1-11), where 41 participants, mostly from industry, drew up high priority R&D recommendations. R. W. Bryers organized the Second International Fouling Conference at White Haven, Pennsylvania, in November 1982 (Reference 1-12); the Engineering Foundation helped organize both the conferences on ash deposits and corrosion from combustion gases and the International Fouling Conference.

DOE also commissioned gas-side fouling surveys of the cement and glass industries, completed in 1982 and 1983 (References 1-13, 14). The latest overall fouling review, with some gas-side material, was given by Knudsen (Reference 1-15) at the Seventh International Heat Transfer Conference in Munich, West Germany, in 1982. Battelle, Pacific Northwest Laboratory (PNL) recently held a DOE-sponsored Fouling and Corrosion Workshop stressing low temperature (below 500 F) gas-side fouling and corrosion (Reference 1-16). As an outgrowth of the Gas-Side Fouling Workshop, Marner and Webb (Reference 1-17) published a gas-side fouling bibliography with a unique classification scheme in 1983, and a second edition of the Battelle Columbus bibliography (Reference 1-1) was in press (Reference 1-18). ASME had also just offered, at the National Heat Transfer Conference in Seattle, a short course on fouling with substantial gas-side content, apparently the first such course in the U.S. (Reference 1-19).

Gas-side fouling is therefore of considerable interest and costs U.S. energy-related industries a considerable sum every year. Despite the work done, many problems remain, and fouling is still described as the "major unresolved problem in heat transfer" (Reference 1-3). This study is part of an effort, run through Battelle, Pacific Northwest Laboratory as prime contractor, to give background to the Office of Industrial Programs (OIP) of DOE for planning a long-term generic R&D program on fouling and corrosion of industrial heat exchangers. The topics of interest are: (a) economic impact of gas-side fouling on plant operation, maintenance and production; (b) prevention, mitigation and accommodation techniques used by industry; (c) startup and shutdown procedures that limit fouling effects; (d) gas-side fouling data in the open literature; (e) heat exchanger design procedures now used to account for fouling; (f) gas-side fouling and corrosion R&D needs as industry sees them; and (g) additional related considerations.

The information was gathered through personal contacts, visits to selected industries and attendance at meetings and conferences, supplemented by publications from the open literature; the literature material concentrates on recent developments and largely expands on what the industrial contacts supplied. Contributors and affiliations are listed in the Acknowledgements, the industrial organizations visited in Appendix A, and the meetings and conferences attended in Appendix B. The survey focuses on gas-side fouling problems in the industrial sector, and the industries of particular interest, listed by Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code (Reference 1-20), appear in Table 1-1.

Table 1-1. Industries Susceptible to Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion Problems. SIC Code 20: Description=Food and Kindred Products; SIC Code 22: Description=Textile Mill Products; SIC Code 26: Description=Paper and Allied Products; SIC Code 28: Description=Chemicals and Allied Products; SIC Code 29: Description=Petroleum Refining and Related Industries; SIC Code 32: Description=Stone, Clay, Glass and Concrete Products; SIC Code 33: Description=Primary Metal Industries; SIC Code 35: Description=Machinery, Except Electrical.

Of these industries, Food and Kindred Products and Textile Mill Products received the least attention in the survey, although both have some reported gas-side fouling problems. In Paper and Allied Products the main problems arise in pulp and paper mills, which routinely burn very large amounts of agricultural wastes. The petrochemical industry, which falls under Chemicals and Allied Products and Petroleum Refining and Related Industries in the SIC scheme, has several notable problems. Within Stone, Clay, Glass and Concrete Products, the glass and cement industries are both heavy energy users with their own fouling problems. Primary Metal Industries are also energy intensive, with the aluminum, copper, and iron and steel industries having the major problems. Machinery, Except Electrical covers gas turbines and Diesel engines, whose exhaust is suitable for heat recovery and is therefore exposed to gas-side fouling and corrosion.

Some aspects of gas-side fouling are specific to particular industries while others are to some degree generic, and the report reflects this. Selected material from non-industrial sources, such as representative marine, utility and municipal applications, is included where it bears on industrial problems, as are selected laboratory-scale results. The problems are also grouped by temperature range: the low-temperature range below 500 F, the intermediate-temperature range from 500 - 1500 F, and the high-temperature range above 1500 F. All three are covered, but the low- and intermediate-temperature ranges get the most attention.

paragraphs.section: 2 A Brief Overview of Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Gas-side fouling is a very broad discipline. The problem starts when fuel is burned in a prime mover or a direct-fired combustion chamber. Depending on the fuel and the combustion process, the resulting combustion gases carry various condensable and non-condensable gaseous components plus some liquid or solid particulate matter. As these hot gases are cooled in a heat exchanger, such as a direct-fired boiler, a waste heat boiler, an economizer or an air preheater, part of the impurities deposit on the heat transfer surface, which generally lowers heat transfer and raises the pressure drop across the exchanger. Such problems occur to some degree in all energy intensive industries, including food, textile, pulp and paper, chemical, petroleum, primary metals, cement and glass, and heat recovery systems on gas turbine and Diesel engine exhausts are also susceptible. This section gives a brief overview, and several topics are expanded in later sections.

Fouling can be defined as an insulating layer of material depositing on a heat-transfer surface; when the deposition takes place from a dirty gas stream it is called gas-side fouling. Often, but not always, gas-side fouling comes together with corrosion, meaning destruction of a metal or alloy through chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment, and/or with erosion, meaning the wearing away of a solid surface by impact of particulate matter carried in the gas stream.

Epstein (Reference 1-7) classifies fouling into six types. (a) Precipitation Fouling: dissolved substances precipitate on the heat transfer surface; when they have inverse rather than normal solubility with temperature, precipitation happens on superheated rather than subcooled surfaces and is often called scaling. (b) Particulate Fouling: finely divided solids suspended in the process fluid accumulate on the surface; in the minority of cases where gravity settling dominates it may be called sedimentation fouling. (c) Chemical Reaction Fouling: deposits form at the surface by chemical reactions in which the surface material is not itself a reactant. (d) Corrosion Fouling: the surface reacts to form corrosion products that foul it and may help other foulants attach. (e) Biological Fouling: macro-organisms (macro-fouling) and/or micro-organisms (micro-biofouling or microbial fouling) attach to the surface, together with the slimes the latter often generate. (f) Solidification Fouling: a liquid or its higher melting constituents freeze onto a subcooled surface. All of these except crystallization fouling can occur on the gas side; particulate fouling is the type most likely to be involved, but chemical reaction fouling, corrosion fouling and solidification can also be important.

Many fuels matter in applications where gas-side fouling may arise. Table 2-1 gives a fuel categorization scheme with 12 categories, a slight modification of that of Marner and Webb (Reference 1-17). Categories 1-6 cover all the important fossil fuels. Category 7 is agricultural wastes, and Category 8 is miscellaneous wastes of the kind burned in municipal incinerators and some industrial applications. Category 9 is process fuels, such as sulfur and phosphorous used to make sulfuric and phosphoric acids. Category 10 covers cases where constituents are added to a fuel or gas to simulate the combustion products of a particular fuel. Category 11 is aerosols, which need not come from combustion but are very important in studies of particulate fouling transport processes. A final miscellaneous category takes cases not covered by the other 11.

The glass industry burns mainly gaseous and petroleum fuels, whereas the cement industry has moved increasingly to coal. Primary metals rely mainly on natural gas, except iron and steel, which gets about three-fourths of its energy from coal and coal-derived fuels. In the machinery group, Diesel engines burn both light and heavy fuel oils, while gas turbines burn mainly gaseous and light petroleum fuels.

Knowing the fuel constituents is central to characterizing combustion gases. Residual oil, for instance, contains sulfur, sodium, vanadium and small amounts of ash, all of which can matter for gas-side fouling. Coal carries substantial ash, containing Al_2O_3, SiO_2 and Fe_2O_3 plus smaller amounts of other constituents, as well as mineral matter such as sulfur and chlorine that contributes to ash deposits and corrosion in coal-fired systems. Because combustion gases contain condensable and corrosive gaseous species, the species present and their dewpoint temperatures are also key. Excess air is a very important parameter: oil- and coal-fired systems keep it low to limit the reaction of SO_2 with oxygen to SO_3, which can then react with H_2O to form H_2SO_4, whereas reciprocating engine exhausts commonly run with 200 to 300 percent excess air.

Combustion gases can carry various particulates depending on the fuel and sometimes on the process. Soot carbon is a frequent particulate in gas turbine and diesel engine exhausts, while Al_2O_3, Fe_2O_3 and SiO_2 are important particulates in coal-fired systems. Besides particulate composition, the particle size distribution and whether the particles are solid or liquid are very important parameters. Fuel treatments, such as premixing the fuel and oxidizer, strongly influence downstream gas-side fouling tendencies, and fuel additives are one mitigation technique, producing softer and more friable deposits than would otherwise form.

The basic phenomena of gas-side fouling are transport to the surface, attachment to it and, in some cases, removal from it. Transport can occur through particle diffusion, vapor diffusion with condensation at the surface, thermophoresis, electrophoresis, diffusiophoresis, inertial impaction, sedimentation and chemical reactions, and in most practical cases two or more act together. Whether a particle sticks when it hits the surface is poorly understood; it is usually expressed as a sticking probability between zero and unity, but predicting it is at present more art than science. Shear stress is a very important parameter in natural removal, as are turbulent bursts, or miniature tornadoes, while deposit strength, which generally rises as the deposit ages, works against the removal forces.

Gas-side fouling deposits are often accompanied by corrosion of the heat-transfer surface, especially in coal-fired systems where alkali-metal sulfates are common. In oil-fired systems vanadium, sulfur and chlorine compounds tend to be corrosive, and where miscellaneous wastes are burned corrosive deposits are a major problem. The term process contaminated gas-side fouling describes situations in which a fuel or combustion gas mixes with raw materials or process streams, giving deposits with constituents other than those from the fuel or its combustion products. One example is the suspension preheater of a cement plant, where pulverized raw feed comes into direct contact with the hot combustion products leaving the rotary kiln.

Dewpoint condensation is a very important deposition mechanism in gas-side fouling. At elevated temperatures, compounds such as Na_2SO_4, K_2SO_4, P_2O_5, Na_2CO_3 and NaCl deposit on heat-transfer surfaces in a variety of important applications. In low-temperature dewpoint condensation, below 500 F, the main constituents of interest are H_2SO_4, HCl and H_2O. Acid deposits are typically highly corrosive and, because the condensate leaves a wet surface, they also capture particulate matter from the gas stream. Low temperature condensation and corrosion are commonly avoided by keeping the surface temperature always above the acid dewpoint temperature of the gas stream.

Materials considerations are very important in several gas-side fouling regimes. Where corrosion is the issue, stainless steels, superalloys, glass and various coatings have been tried with varying success, and ceramic materials attract considerable interest for withstanding hostile dirty-gas environments at elevated temperatures, i.e., greater than 1500 F. There is also considerable interest in gas-side fouling predictive methods, but the gas-side state of the art lags far behind that for liquids, and such methods will not appear until more gas-side fouling data are obtained over a broad range of governing parameters.

paragraphs.section: 2.5 Design of Heat-Transfer Equipment for Gas-Side Fouling Service
paragraphs.text: Heat-transfer equipment for gas-side fouling service falls into five main categories: (a) recuperators, (b) regenerators, (c) fluidized bed exchangers, (d) direct contact exchangers and (e) heat pipe exchangers. Recuperators are all conventional heat exchangers in which a solid surface, usually a metal or alloy, separates the two fluids; examples are direct-fired boilers, fired heaters, waste heat boilers, economizers, air preheaters and superheaters. They are usually tubular, but other geometries such as plate fin compact heat exchangers also belong here. Tubular units are called firetube boilers when the hot gases flow inside the tubes and watertube boilers when the gases flow across the tubebanks. Regenerators are transient type exchangers of two basic kinds: (a) a rotating wheel with a core matrix, with hot and cold gases flowing through opposite sides of the wheel in counterflow, and (b) a stationary matrix through which hot and cold gases are routed alternately.

paragraphs.section: 2.5 Design of Heat-Transfer Equipment for Gas-Side Fouling Service
paragraphs.text: A fluidized bed heat exchanger has a fluidized bed on its hot side that heats a gas or liquid flowing in the tubes. The bed material, sometimes sand, scours the outside of the tubes and so tends to mitigate gas-side fouling; finned rather than plain tubes are frequently used in these units. Direct contact heat exchangers let the two heat transfer media meet directly with no solid surface between them; an industrial example is the cement-industry suspension preheater, which preheats pulverized raw feed before it enters the rotary kiln for calcining. Heat pipes are used in selected industrial heat recovery applications. Because each heat pipe is essentially an isothermal tube, the exchanger is a bundle of individually sealed heat pipes divided by a partition in the middle of the bundle, perpendicular to it; hot gases flow on one side of the partition, and cold gases are heated as they flow over the hot tube ends at the opposite end of the unit.

paragraphs.section: 2.5 Design of Heat-Transfer Equipment for Gas-Side Fouling Service
paragraphs.text: The classical design approach for gas-side fouling is to oversurface the heat exchanger through the fouling factor concept. However, very few fouling factors are available, so experience-based values are used, and where heavy fouling occurs, provision for regular cleaning must also be made. For tubular exchangers the designer can choose plain or finned tubes; with finned tubes, important parameters for fouling potential include fin height, fin spacing, fin thickness and fin material. Layout geometry is another important parameter, and where soot blowers are used, inline layouts are usually chosen for easier cleaning. Further design options, including materials choice, are taken up in Section 3.

paragraphs.section: 2.6 Operation and Cleaning of Heat-Transfer Equipment in Dirty Gas Environments
paragraphs.text: Cleaning techniques are a very important consideration where gas-side fouling is a problem, and with heavy deposits cleaning generally has to be done online while the unit is in service. Sootblowers using dry steam or air as the blowing medium are the most widely used technique, and low frequency and high frequency sonic sootblowers, or sonic horns, have attracted considerable recent attention. Water washing is another very important technique, and other methods include chemical, mechanical and thermal cleaning. Matching the cleaning technique to the deposit type is essential to optimize cleaning and minimize cost. Gas additives are widely used to mitigate fouling; MgO has undoubtedly been the most widely used and most successful additive for both oil and coal-fired systems, and its particle size distribution, which relates to its surface area, is an important parameter.

paragraphs.section: 2.6 Operation and Cleaning of Heat-Transfer Equipment in Dirty Gas Environments
paragraphs.text: The best source of gas-side fouling information is often general field operating experience, including problems tied to startup, off-design and shutdown conditions. Many case histories are documented in the literature, with direct-fired coal boilers receiving the most attention, though experience from heat recovery systems recently installed in various exhaust gas streams has also been documented. A final consideration is the economic impact of gas-side fouling. Its harmful effects are well known, but quantifying the contributing factors is extremely difficult, so relatively little is known about gas-side fouling costs in U.S. industries.

paragraphs.section: 3 Heat-Exchanger Design for Gas-Side Fouling Service
paragraphs.text: Designers have a number of tools for handling potential gas-side fouling problems. Because design and operation go hand-in-hand, this section includes a significant amount of relevant field experience, particularly as it bears on design. It covers three main topics: (a) the role of the fouling factor, (b) the various types of heat transfer equipment and (c) materials considerations. Figures of representative industrial heat exchangers illustrate the physical units in which fouling actually occurs, and the materials discussion is split into the three temperature ranges defined in Section 1.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 The Role of the Fouling Factor
paragraphs.text: Q = F U_o A_o LMTD (3-1) (heat duty = LMTD correction factor × overall heat transfer coefficient × total outside surface area × logarithmic mean temperature difference). The classical way to deal with fouling is the fouling factor, or fouling resistance, R_f. For a heat exchanger in which a solid surface separates two fluids, Eq. 3-1 gives the heat transferred between them, where Q is the heat duty, F is the LMTD correction factor, U_o is the overall heat transfer coefficient, A_o is the total outside surface area, and LMTD is the logarithmic mean temperature difference between the two fluids.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 The Role of the Fouling Factor
paragraphs.text: 1/U_oA_o = 1/h_iA_i + t_w/k_wA_w + 1/h_oA_o + R_fi/A_i + R_fo/A_o (3-2) (total thermal resistance = inside convection + wall conduction + outside convection + inside fouling + outside fouling resistance). In Eq. 3-2, h_i and h_o are the inside and outside convective heat transfer coefficients, A_i is the inside surface area, t_w is the wall thickness, k_w is the wall thermal conductivity, A_w is the average wall surface area, and R_fi and R_fo are the inside and outside fouling resistances. The equation shows that fouling resistances lower U_o and therefore Q. To offset this expected loss of thermal performance, extra surface area is specified, the amount depending on the fouling factor value used and on the size of the other resistances in Eq. 3-2.

paragraphs.section: 3.1 The Role of the Fouling Factor
paragraphs.text: At initial startup, when the unit is clean, running at design conditions gives gas temperatures somewhat below the design values. If gas velocity is reduced to compensate, the shear stresses in the gas also drop, which reduces the fouling removal forces and actually encourages gas-side fouling. Fouling factors are clearly transient and involve very complicated mechanisms: beginning from a clean surface, fouling grows until, depending on the mechanisms, an asymptotic condition may be reached in which deposition equals removal. Constant fouling factors are generally used for design, and the subject is treated further in Section 4.

Broadly, heat-transfer equipment is either direct fired, such as boilers and fired heaters, or waste heat recovery equipment. Waste heat recovery equipment falls into two broad categories (Reference 3-1): units essential for process control, such as a firetube boiler used in producing sulfuric or phosphoric acid in a chemical plant, and units justified by economics, such as an air preheater on a boiler or a waste heat boiler on gas turbine exhaust. For discussion here, the exchangers in which gas-side fouling can be a problem are grouped as (a) recuperators, (b) regenerators, (c) direct contact exchangers, (d) fluidized bed exchangers and (e) heat pipe exchangers, each presented with relevant fouling experience and illustrations.

Recuperators are conventional two-fluid heat exchangers in which a solid, usually some metal or alloy, separates the fluids, though glass and plastics are also used to a limited extent. Many types are made, generally designed for steady state operation and serving many industrial functions. Shell-and-Tube Exchangers: the shell-and-tube heat exchanger (Figure 3-1, Reference 3-2) is probably the best example of a recuperator. It comes in all sizes and shapes and serves a broad range of applications, for example (a) a vertical steam generator using fluid catalytic cracker off-gases in the petroleum industry, (b) a transfer line exchanger recovering heat from thermal cracking for olefins production in ethylene plants in the chemical industry, and (c) a gas-to-air heat recovery system using combustion products from a sewage sludge incinerator. Many firetube boilers are also special cases of the shell-and-tube exchanger.

Figure 3-1. The Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchanger (Reference 3-2), drawn with a numbered component nomenclature. Figure 3-2. A Schematic Diagram of a Steam Power Plant (Reference 3-3). Figure 3-3. A Cylindrical Economizer with Rotary Sootblower (Reference 3-4).

The watertube boiler, usually just called a boiler, is another of the most common recuperators. An industrial boiler consists of the boiler surface, usually together with a superheater, an economizer that preheats the boiler feedwater, and an air preheater that uses exhaust gases to preheat combustion air, as sketched in Figure 3-2 (Reference 3-3). Figure 3-3 (Reference 3-4) shows an economizer designed for stack installation, with a rotary-element sootblower at its bottom and finned tubes. Fluids other than water can be used tubeside: organic liquids such as toluene are common working fluids in intermediate temperature Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycles (ORBC) recovering heat from gas turbine and Diesel engine exhausts. Other industrial boilers include enhanced oil recovery (EOR) steamers in the petroleum industry, waste incineration boilers in the chemical industry and recovery boilers in the pulp and paper industry. Most boilers have steam sootblowers for online cleaning of external surfaces.

Kraft pulp mills widely use boilers fired with black liquor (spent liquor from the cooking process) and hog fuel (bark, wood chips and related wastes) as primary fuels. The spent black liquor is concentrated and burned in large recovery boilers, which usually have two superheaters. In the lower superheater, deposits come mainly from carry over, or inertial impaction, of particulate matter in the combusted gases and consist chiefly of Na_2SO_4 and Na_2CO_3, with smaller amounts of NaCl, NaOH, potassium salts and reduced sulfur compounds. In the upper superheater and on the boiler surface, deposits form mainly by vapor condensation of Na_2SO_4, NaCl and a little Na_2CO_3 (Reference 3-5).

A colloquium on gas-side fouling in kraft pulp mills was held at the University of Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on October 28, 1982 (Reference 3-6). Forty-two representatives, mainly from industry, discussed unit plugging experience, R&D on deposit formation and characteristics, ways to prevent and control deposit accumulation, and how deposits relate to boiler design and operation. The discussions confirmed that the physical character of the deposits depends strongly on flue gas temperature. In the lower superheater, exposed to high gas temperatures, deposits are fused, hard, dense, bonded to the tubes and hard to remove with sootblowers. In the upper superheater and on the boiler surface (gas temperatures 900 - 1200 F) deposits are generally white and, depending on temperature, either hard and dense or porous and friable. Further back in the unit they are usually white, powdery and easily removed by sootblowers.

Several design measures have been used to address these recovery boiler problems: (a) superheater side spacing increased from 10 to 12 in. to reduce plugging; (b) center spacing in the first four boiler rows doubled from 4.5 to 9.0 in.; (c) close attention to good tube alignment; (d) careful velocity control, always below 25 ft/sec near the boiler surface and below 15 ft/sec in the superheat regions; (e) flue gas temperature control, with a maximum of 1700 F entering the superheater region and 1100 - 1300 F entering the boiler bank; and (f) proper distribution of primary, secondary and tertiary air.

Unlike the watertube boiler, a firetube boiler carries the hot gases inside the tubes; an example (Reference 3-7) appears in Figure 3-4. Turbulators are often placed in the tubes to raise the gas-side transfer coefficients, which are much lower than those for boiling water or other liquid on the shellside. Typical applications are (a) waste heat recovery in sulfuric acid plants, (b) removal of sulfur compounds from sulfur plant tail gas with waste heat recovery, in the chemical industry, and (c) process gas cooling after steam/methane reforming furnaces in the petroleum industry. In some dirty-gas services firetube boilers are chosen because they make off-line mechanical cleaning of the tube interiors easier, and walnut shells or similar abrasive materials are often used for online scouring. Where combustion gases carry large amounts of abrasive particulates that would badly erode external surfaces in cross flow, firetube boilers are also common, with ferrules or sleeves usually fitted in the tube inlets to resist erosion as the gas leaves the header and enters the tubes.

In some processes, such as sulfuric acid production, outlet gas temperature control is essential; for a firetube boiler it is done with an internal or external bypass (Figure 3-5, Reference 3-1). In the contact method for H_2SO_4, raw sulfur is burned with air in a combustion chamber to give SO_2, O_2 and N_2 at about 1900 F and 50 in. H_2O. These gases are cooled to about 800 F in a waste heat boiler that raises steam, then pass to a converter where SO_2 is oxidized to SO_3 over catalysts, possibly in stages, so that most SO_2 has become SO_3 after the last stage. The SO_3 gases, at around 900 F because the exothermic SO_2 --> SO_3 reaction heats them by 50 - 100 F, are cooled in an economizer and then absorbed in diluted sulfuric acid in an absorption tower to form concentrated H_2SO_4. Exit gas temperature control is critical here: the bypass adjusts flow through the boiler so that at lower loads, when gas temperature falls, mixing hot bypass gas with the cooler boiler gas still gives the desired exit temperature.
Figure 3-4. A Two-Pass Firetube Boiler (Reference 3-7). Figure 3-5. External and Internal Bypass in Firetube Boiler for Exit Gas Temperature Control (Reference 3-1).

Figure 3-6 (Reference 3-8) shows a gas-to-air recuperator that cools hot exhaust gases from a suspension preheater in the cement industry. Hot gas enters the top at 700 F, flows down inside the tubes and goes on to the baghouse, while the air is designed to make four passes over the outside of the tube bundle before leaving at 400 F. The cement industry also uses this exchanger type to cool exhaust from clinker coolers and preheater bypass streams. The units are very large, with tubes typically 20 to 40 ft long. In these crossflow exchangers the tubes are typically 3 in. in diameter on an inline layout with longitudinal pitch smaller than transverse pitch. The hot, dirty gas is put tubeside to allow off-line mechanical cleaning if needed, and a replaceable sleeve five diameters long is fitted at the tube inlet against inlet erosion; these inserts matter especially in clinker cooler service, where the exhaust is highly abrasive.

At one installation in a preheater application at the Monarch Cement Company in Humboldt, Kansas, an interesting problem arose (Reference 3-9): the gas-to-air exchanger developed a 1/4-in. buildup of particulate matter from the gas stream inside the tubes within a very short time. After extensive analysis it was concluded that static charges picked up by the particles in the suspension preheater were mainly responsible for this gas-side fouling. Suspension preheater operation is described further in Section 3.2.3 on direct contact heat exchangers.

Gas-side heat transfer coefficients are relatively low compared with those for liquids and phase change, so extended surfaces are widely used to enhance tubular exchangers in gas-side service by adding tube surface area. The fins are helically wrapped and welded and are typically solid or segmented (Figure 3-7, Reference 3-10); round and elliptical studs are also used, though less widely. Augmentation of gas-to-gas heat exchangers is effective only if both sides are enhanced, whereas gas-to-liquid exchangers need enhancement only on the gas side.

The relative cleanability of segmented and solid fins is controversial. Csathy (Reference 3-11) prefers segmented fins for their slightly lower weight and, in most practical cases, slightly higher heat absorption for the same fin configuration, and also because they stay cleaner: segment edges cut larger particles into pieces and sootblower steam jets can reach the fin root through the cuts, whereas the shaded area behind plain fins is hard to reach; he adds that narrower segments clean even more easily. Smittle (Reference 3-12) argues that, although serrated fins give somewhat better heat transfer, soot quickly collects in the serrations and cleaning becomes a real problem, so only solid fins are recommended in dirty gas streams from oil, coal, wood or other high-fouling fuels. DeAnda (Reference 3-13) found that in No. 6 Diesel fuel exhausts segmented and solid finned tubes fouled at about the same rate, so fouling and cleaning of plain versus segmented finned tubes need further study.

Fin type, fin thickness, fin height and number of fins per unit length are all important parameters. As a general rule, the dirtier the fuel, the wider the fin spacing: coal-fired systems should use no more than three fins per inch, while six fins per inch is customary for natural gas. Finned tubebanks are used in crossflow exchangers with the dirty gas outside the tubes, and the layout, staggered or inline (Figure 3-8), is another important parameter. Profos and Sharon (Reference 3-14) state that inline tubebanks are easier to clean mechanically, while sootblowers are about equally effective for both arrangements; even so, most engineers specify inline layouts when sootblowers are required, and a wider pitch is customary for dirtier fuels. Inline layouts carry a severe heat-transfer penalty with finned tubes: Weierman, Taborek and Marner (Reference 3-15) tested several segmented-finned-tube bundles under clean, unfouled conditions and found that four staggered rows performed about as well as seven inline rows.

Figure 3-6. A Gas-to-Air Heat Exchanger Used in the Cement Industry (Reference 3-8). Figure 3-7. Solid and Segmented Welded Finned Tubes (Reference 3-10). Figure 3-8. A Comparison of Inline Versus Staggered Layouts (Reference 3-10).

The plate-fin exchanger is a compact surface long used in the aerospace and automotive industries that has recently drawn great interest for heat recovery. Harrison Radiator Division (Reference 3-16) and AiResearch Manufacturing Company (References 3-17, 3-18) both developed high-performance plate-fin recuperators for industry, although Harrison has since dropped its product line because of current economic conditions (Reference 3-19). AiResearch's family of high-performance metallic recuperators is meant for industrial gas streams up to 1500 F and uses a counterflow arrangement with crossflow end sections for fluid manifolding and a compact brazed plate-fin structure. In the typical matrix (Figure 3-9, Reference 3-18), parallel plates form the flow passages and corrugated sheet fins between them enhance heat transfer, with ferritic stainless steel used for both plates and fins. An offset rectangular fin pattern is used for relatively clean gases, and a plain fin with relatively open passages is offered for dirty combustion gases where fouling is a major concern.

The plate-fin recuperator was demonstrated starting in 1978 on flue gases from a reverberatory aluminum remelt furnace at the AiResearch Casting Company, operating for three years with average fuel savings of 31 percent. The Garrett plate-fin recuperator has also been installed on a steel plant annealing furnace and a steel casting car bottom furnace, and in clay and grain drying operations. Further operating and cleaning experience with the Garrett plate-fin heat recovery system is given in Sections 5 and 6. Figure 3-9. Plate-Fin Heat Exchanger Construction (Reference 3-18).

paragraphs.section: 3.2.1 Recuperators / Exchangers for Fluid Catalytic Cracker Units (FCCU)
paragraphs.text: In petroleum refining, catalytic cracking breaks heavy fractions, mainly gas oils, into lower molecular weight fractions, and fluid bed processes use a finely powdered catalyst in a fluid bed for this thermal decomposition (Reference 2-1). The catalyst is regenerated from time to time by burning off deposited carbon at 1000 - 1400 F and pressures up to 30 psig, so the regenerator flue gases, which usually carry large amounts of catalyst fines and carbon monoxide, CO, are hot, pressurized and combustible and suit heat recovery; FCCU fouling experience is therefore treated separately. At the Mobil Oil Refinery in Torrance, California, which burns almost only natural gas, the only gas-side fouling problem is at the FCCU (Reference 3-20). The CO-rich regenerator gases are burned in a CO boiler and the heat is used to raise steam in a waste heat boiler whose first few rows are smooth tubes shielding the remaining finned tubes from direct impact of catalyst fines, some of which still deposit at the fin roots. The exit temperature is held above 300 F to avoid acid and water dewpoint problems, but the sootblowers, run once per shift, do not clean the finned tubes satisfactorily.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.1 Recuperators / Exchangers for Fluid Catalytic Cracker Units (FCCU)
paragraphs.text: Krowech (Reference 3-21) reported a case study of a FCCU at another refinery. Gases were available for heat recovery at 1325 F and 7 psig and held 0.23 grains/SCF of catalyst fines, mainly alumina typically under 20 microns, which can be very erosive depending on gas velocity and flow arrangement. The plant's vertical firetube units suffered many mechanical failures and their exhaust gas temperature was too high, so a water quench was needed before the electrostatic precipitator; the firetubes were scoured with walnut shells every other shift. They were replaced by longitudinal flow watertube exchangers with a crossflow superheater and sootblowers, designed for high downflow velocity to minimize fouling and erosion since the tubes had longitudinal fins. Sonic sootblowers seemed well suited to the pressurized environment, but difficulties arose and the horns did not clean effectively. Despite earlier erosion problems, regular walnut shell scouring was resumed, with boiler and superheater scoured once every three days, which kept the unit sufficiently clean.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.1 Recuperators / Exchangers for Fluid Catalytic Cracker Units (FCCU)
paragraphs.text: After one year the boiler was shut down for maintenance and inspection. The horizontal superheater tubes in crossflow had fines deposits up to 1/3-in. thick in low flow areas, while in high-flow areas the tubes were clean, polished and somewhat eroded; the boiler showed no erosion. Krowech concluded that where erosion is a concern, flow parallel to surfaces can tolerate higher velocities than flow normal to them: 105 ft/sec caused no erosion at all in longitudinal flow, whereas similar velocities in crossflow polished and eroded the tubes to some extent. The designer for gas-side fouling service therefore has to estimate two key parameters: the stable deposit thickness, which sets the fin spacing needed to prevent bridging (deposits touching between fins), which severely degrades heat transfer; and the gas-side fouling factor, needed to size the surface area. Gas velocity, surface orientation and cleaning techniques can then be combined with prior operating experience for successful design.

Regenerators are transient, or unsteady, heat-transfer devices of two basic types, rotating and stationary. In the rotary regenerative heater (Figure 3-10), a rotor turns slowly within a box housing, with hot gases flowing through one side and air through the other in counterflow. The stationary type uses a fixed matrix: hot gases first flow through and heat it, then air is heated passing through the same matrix, so hot and cold fluids alternate. Dirty gases tend to plug the small regenerator passages, so regenerators generally have both sootblowers and water washing capability. An important rotary example is the Ljungstrom air preheater, widely used to preheat boiler combustion air, which is particularly vulnerable to gas-side fouling and corrosion from sulfuric acid condensing at its low-temperature end. Figure 3-10. The Rotary Regenerator (Reference 3-22).

An important stationary-matrix application is heat recovery from melting furnace exhaust in the glass industry (Reference 1-14). Because glass melts at high temperature, exhaust leaves the melting furnace at about 2800 F, and most plants use brick-checkers-type periodic flow regenerators to recover heat for preheating combustion air. The gases leave the checkers at 1000 - 1200 F and are vented, as the glass industry currently uses no secondary heat recovery. The hot gases are extremely corrosive with a tremendous fouling potential, the main constituents responsible being SiO_2, Na_2SO_4, Al_2O_3, V_2O_5 and CaSO_4. In the top, hottest zone of the regenerator, fouling and corrosion stem mainly from SiO_2, V_2O_5, brick erosion and large particulates; in the bottom zone SO_3 is the main corrosion cause and condensed Na_2SO_4 the main fouling cause. Typical effects are erosion, sticky eutectics, weakening and crumbling of bricks, particulate deposition and slag formation. Webb and Kulkarni (Reference 1-14) identify remedies: (a) additives such as MgO and carbon, (b) control of operating conditions such as excess combustion air, (c) high quality fuels such as natural gas and electric boosting, and (d) batch treatment such as pelletizing, briquetting, moisturizing and preheating.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.3 Direct Contact Heat Exchangers / Suspension Preheaters
paragraphs.text: Direct contact heat exchangers (DCHX) bring the two heat-transfer media into direct contact without a separating solid surface, which makes them one possible way to avoid, or at least reduce, gas-side fouling. Their applications are fairly limited, and two examples are discussed. About one-half of U.S. dry process cement kilns now have suspension preheaters; the widely used Fuller-Humboldt system is shown in Figure 3-11 (Reference 3-23). It has four cyclones, or stages, each with a long riser in which raw feed is carried up into the cyclone in parallel with hot gas from the preceding cyclone, so heat passes directly from the hot kiln exhaust to the cooler feed held in suspension. The raw material takes only about 30 seconds to pass through the whole preheater and reaches about 1475 F, and about 45 percent of the total required calcination (driving CO_2 from CaCO_3 to give CaO, the main constituent of portland cement) happens in the preheater. Some preheaters also have a precalciner (PC in Figure 3-11), an auxiliary fuel burning chamber that allows a shorter kiln.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.3 Direct Contact Heat Exchangers / Suspension Preheaters
paragraphs.text: Although raw feed and kiln gas are not separated by a surface, severe buildups still form on the cyclone separator surfaces, requiring periodic shutdown for mechanical cleaning. Vaporized alkalies, sulfates and chlorides in the kiln gas can condense on the raw feed in the preheater, return to the kiln, re-volatilize and repeat the cycle, so a bypass (Figure 3-11) is often used to limit their buildup in the kiln-preheater system. In addition, strong particle interaction in the preheater can charge the particles electrically, so if the preheater exit gas enters a heat exchanger such as the gas-to-air unit of Figure 3-6, particulates may deposit on the heat-transfer surfaces by electrophoresis; References 3-24 and 1-13 discuss these and related problems further.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.3 Direct Contact Heat Exchangers / Low-Temperature Direct Contact Heat Exchanger
paragraphs.text: Heat recovery below 300 F is generally avoided because acids and water condense on metallic surfaces below their dewpoints, causing fouling and corrosion. Much of this low-level energy can nevertheless be recovered by condensing the water vapor in the exhaust and using it for feed water heating, air preheating or process hot water; the technique is considered new in the U.S. but many installations already run in Europe. In the basic process (Figure 3-12, Reference 3-25), flue gas typically enters the direct contact heat exchanger above 300 F, passes straight through the cold water stream in the spray chamber and leaves the top at 100 to 120 F, much like a cooling tower working in reverse: the gas is cooled and the recovered energy supplies hot water. Because the water becomes contaminated by exhaust constituents, a secondary heat exchanger normally transfers the recovered heat to the process fluid. A major advantage of the DCHX is that no solid surface resists heat flow, so many fluids can be handled under conditions that would foul and corrode a conventional exchanger.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.3 Direct Contact Heat Exchangers / Low-Temperature Direct Contact Heat Exchanger
paragraphs.text: Corrosion in such a condensing unit can usually be prevented by building the tower, pump and secondary heat exchanger from Type 304 or 316 stainless steel or fiberglass reinforced plastic. A distinctive feature of this DCHX is that it lowers emissions while recovering energy; SO_2 emissions, for example, can be cut considerably with an alkaline water spray. KVB, Inc., Irvine, California (References 3-26 and 3-27) has recently begun marketing in the U.S. a condensation heat recovery unit for new or retrofit natural gas-fired boilers, made entirely of corrosion-resistant Type 316 stainless steel, whereas 500 such installations already operate in Europe.

paragraphs.section: 3.2.3 Direct Contact Heat Exchangers / Low-Temperature Direct Contact Heat Exchanger
paragraphs.text: Two West German installations illustrate the approach. At a slaughterhouse boiler, the hot water serves the packing process and washing down meat processing equipment; at full load the flue gas is cooled from 450 F to about 140 F, heating incoming plant water from 50 to over 100 F. In a chemical plant, a two-stage flue gas heat recovery unit on a 30,000 lbm/hr boiler cools the flue gas from 410 to 120 F, enough to raise inlet feedwater temperature from 50 to 155 F; when it was installed in 1980, the fuel savings gave a payback of just over one year.
Figure 3-11. Suspension Preheater Used in the Cement Industry (Reference 3-23). Figure 3-12. Low-Temperature Direct Contact Heat Exchanger (Reference 3-25).

Rudnicki, Mah and Williams (Reference 3-28) recently gave an excellent review of fluidized bed heat exchangers (FBHX) for heat recovery; shallow bed FBHXs in particular have been studied widely and found competitive with conventional heat exchangers. Waste heat recovery design is limited by low gas-side heat transfer coefficients, which lead to large surface areas: a typical waste heat recovery boiler has about four times the surface area of a typical liquid-to-liquid exchanger for the same duty. Fluidized beds therefore offer several potential advantages: enhanced heat transfer, with coefficients up to 20 to 25 times gas-side coefficients; self cleaning, since the bed particles gently scrub the heat-transfer surfaces, finned tubes included; and pollution control, since the bed can filter unwanted particulates from the exhaust and the bed material can be chosen to absorb gaseous pollutants such as SO_2.

Stone-Platt Fluidfire, Ltd. in the United Kingdom developed a shallow bed FBHX (Figure 3-13) in which gas flows up through a distributor plate and the bed material, typically silica sand or aluminum oxide, producing a very high gas-side heat transfer coefficient. Plugging and corrosion of the distributor plate slots can be a serious problem in this design, so chain-driven steel brushes periodically remove accumulated deposits. Stone-Platt installed such a unit on the Shell International Marine tanker Fjordshell, a 32,000 ton ship, as a waste heat boiler on the exhaust of the 900 kW Diesel engine driving the ship. This unit, the largest industrial FBHX in operation, measures about 9 ft by 12 ft by 18 ft high and contains three parallel shallow beds with a total bed area of almost 325 ft^2, its distributor plate cleaned by steel brushes. Stone-Platt has about 20 other FBHX installations, including a ceramic plant tunnel kiln exhaust, a steel plant galvanizing bath exhaust, a steel plant heat-treat furnace, and an economizer in a chemical plant. Figure 3-13. A Schematic Drawing of a Fluidized Bed Heat Recovery System (Reference 3-29).

The Aerojet Energy Conversion Company, Sacramento, California, is conducting a FBHX study on aluminum remelt furnace exhaust at an aluminum plant in New York State (Reference 3-30), using a shallow bed unit of the type described above. The fuels are natural gas and No. 6 fuel oil; besides fuel contaminants such as vanadium and sulfur from the oil, the flue gas carries melt carry-over including aluminum oxide, aluminum sulfate and vanadates. Objectives are to determine the gas-side fouling characteristics of the distributor plate in this exhaust, to see how well the FBHX performs at gas temperatures up to 1800 F, and to study fouling and corrosion of the exhaust using a temperature controlled probe. The probe is a circular cylinder of nine segments, so that several materials can be evaluated in a single insertion into the exhaust gases.

Heat pipes transfer heat under essentially isothermal conditions. A heat pipe is a sealed tube holding a fluid with a predetermined boiling point: the hot stream boils this liquid so that hot vapor fills the tube, the vapor travels to the cold zone where it gives heat to the cold stream and condenses, and a wick inside the tube returns the liquid to the hot portion. This vaporizing and condensing cycle continues as long as the two ends are exposed to hot and cold streams; in effect the heat pipe is a boiler with the wick acting as the pump. For heat recovery a bundle of finned tube heat pipes may be used, with hot exhaust gases flowing over one end of the bundle and the air to be heated over the other (Fig. 3-14, Reference 3-31). Figure 3-14. Schematic Drawing of a Heat Pipe Heat Recovery System (Reference 3-31).

In late 1979 a manufacturing facility at the Monsanto Chocolate Bayou Plant put on stream what is thought to be the first large industrial heat pipe application (Reference 3-32). The air preheaters, part of a major energy modernization project, used finned steel heat pipes with a napthalene toluene mixture as working fluid. They served five natural gas process heaters with a combined heat duty of 150 MM Btu/hr (1M = 10^3), all designed to lower flue gas exit temperature from 750 F to 375 F, with individual exchanger duties between 4.4 MM Btu/hr and 1.5 MM Btu/hr. The project also added O_2 analyzers to control excess air, and startup was completed in early 1980 with better heat-transfer performance than expected.

After slightly over three years of operation the units were opened for the first time in June 1983 for inspection and water washing. Neither side showed any visible change, although a 15 percent drop in heat-transfer performance had been observed, which Monsanto personnel attributed more to changed operating conditions than to fouling. About two hard hats full of dirt were found at the bottom of the combustion air duct; it may have come off the heat pipes through static charge dissipation and mechanical vibration during the 36-hr duct disassembly. The furnaces with heat pipes also have particulate fouling in the convection section, where refractory and iron oxide particles from the firebox collect at the fin roots without degrading thermal performance.

Specifying materials for industrial heat-transfer equipment in gas-side fouling service is a very important design option. Characterizing the combustion gases, including gaseous species, temperature, velocity, particle loading, particle composition and particle size distribution, is a key input to material selection. Some gas-side fouling deposits are highly corrosive even at low temperatures, and gases carrying abrasive particles can cause severe erosion without proper precautions. Temperature level is especially important because deposition processes usually depend on both gas temperature and surface temperature. As in Section 1, the discussion is split into three regimes: (a) low-temperature range, T_gas < 500 F; (b) intermediate-temperature range, 500 F < T_gas < 1500 F; and (c) high-temperature range, which the original prints here as T_gas < 1500 F.

The classic problem in this regime is acid and water dewpoint condensation. Oil, coal and many other fuels contain sulfur, which combines with oxygen during combustion to form sulfur dioxide, SO_2, and, given enough excess air, sulfur trioxide, SO_3. SO_3 can combine with water to form sulfuric acid, H_2SO_4, which condenses on heat transfer surfaces colder than the acid dewpoint temperature. Under normal operating conditions the sulfuric acid dewpoint is about 240 to 280 F depending on the SO_3 content of the gases. At still lower surface temperatures, water condenses in the 110 to 150 F range and can combine with SO_3 to form sulfurous acid, which, like H_2SO_4, can be highly corrosive. Surface temperatures are kept above the water dewpoint in most applications, but acid dewpoint condensation is a serious problem for low-temperature heat recovery.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Predicting the Acid Dewpoint Temperature
paragraphs.text: Figure 3-15 (Reference 3-33) plots the acid dewpoint temperature of fuel oil combustion gases against the percentage of sulfur in the fuel, together with representative experimental data and the API RP 533 (Reference 3-34) recommendation for air preheaters, which lies on the high side of the data. A design based on this guideline will probably avoid dewpoint condensation because the method is conservative, but it will also keep heat recovery surfaces hotter than necessary, so the exhausted gases still carry recoverable energy. This is the designer's dilemma: the surface temperature should exceed the dewpoint to avoid acid condensation, yet the gas temperature should be as low as possible to recover as much energy as possible. Figure 3-15. Acid Dewpoint Temperature of Combustion Gases from Fuel Oil as a Function of Sulfur Content (Reference 3-33).

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Cold End Corrosion in the Ljungstrom Preheater
paragraphs.text: Ljungstrom air preheaters are rotary regenerators widely used to preheat combustion air. Sotter (Reference 3-35) notes that many regenerative preheaters are in poor condition due to corrosion, giving a typical service life of about two years. Corten, which resists corrosion well, is the most common air preheater material, and Type 409 stainless steel is used to some extent. C E - Air Preheater, a subsidiary of Combustion Engineering, used porcelain enameled heat transfer surfaces in oil-fired service so that surface temperatures could run below the levels safe for metallic materials (Reference 3-36). Cold end corrosion is a bigger problem in oil-fired than in coal-fired systems because (a) vanadium in residual oil-ash deposits catalyzes conversion of SO_2 to SO_3, and (b) ash in flue gas tends to lower the SO_3 vapor content, but oils contain far less ash than coal.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Coatings to Resist Cold End Corrosion
paragraphs.text: Miller et al. (Reference 3-37) at Argonne National Laboratory surveyed possible plastic heat exchangers for situations such as the acid dewpoint problem, citing chemical inertness, versatile fabrication methods, moisture resistance and corrosion resistance as advantages. They selected three candidates for further study, (a) polytetrafluoroethylene (Teflon), (b) polyphenylene (Ryton) and (c) polyvinylidene fluoride (Kynar), with Teflon as the leading one. An AiResearch laboratory study (Reference 3-13), placing samples in a concentrated acid bath printed as "H_SO_4" [subscript 판독 불가], confirmed that Teflon, Ryton and Kynar would all be good coating candidates for heat exchanger surfaces exposed to cold end corrosion, provided sharp edges, burrs and other protrusions are first removed by filing, blasting, peening, pickling, etc.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Coatings to Resist Cold End Corrosion
paragraphs.text: Dyer (Reference 3-38) reports that Kentube applied a ceramic coating to finned tubes for a cold end corrosion application: the surface was mechanically cleaned, pickled and dipped in a bath to give a coating about 1 - 2 mils thick. The coating tended to chip and proved ineffective in abrasive environments, and its thermal shock response was not determined. Weierman (Reference 3-39) reports hot-dip galvanizing the outside of a carbon-steel finned-tube bundle to resist corrosion in a unit where a water spray on the bundle exterior enhanced heat transfer by evaporative cooling and the water inside the tubes cooled foundry equipment.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Glass-Tube Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: Glass-tube heat exchangers look very promising for low-temperature heat recovery where fouling and corrosion are potential problems; experience with units from two manufacturers is reported, most installations being in Europe with a few now in the U.S. Air Froehlich in the United Kingdom developed a glass tube recuperator for gas temperatures below 500 F with excellent corrosion resistance, used in textile, ceramics, foodstuffs, chemical, and pulp and paper industries (Table 3-1, Reference 3-40). One long-running example is in a textile plant: on a textile finishing machine with cylinder dryers, fumes and vapor are drawn through a hood over the dryers and exhausted, and must be replaced by outside air preheated to 68 - 77 F for workspace ventilation, with a bypass in the exhaust gas duct controlling supply air temperature in warmer seasons to avoid overheating the plant. The plant chose a glass-tube recuperator to heat this air with the exhaust, mainly because of the fouling potential of the hood exhaust, which carries dust, fibers and sticky finishing components that deposit outside the tubes near the inlet, or coolest, side. A permanently installed sprinkler nozzle flushes the deposits periodically, and the absence of fouling problems was credited to the fine glass surface structure, the high gas velocity and periodic cleaning.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Glass-Tube Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: Corning Glass Works (References 3-41, 3-42) recently developed modular gas-to-gas to gas-to-liquid heat recovery systems for low grade energy. They are currently limited to maximum gas temperatures of about 500 to 550 F because sealing relies on a special elastomer, and Corning hopes to raise the limit to about 800 F by developing ceramic seals. These "Pyrotherm" systems are built from modular banks of Pyrex brand borosilicate glass tubes with stainless steel headers, the dirty gas always on the tubeside; tubes are typically 1.0 in. in diameter with a 0.030-in. wall. Pyrex conducts heat less well than most exchanger metals, but the inner and outer gas-side convective coefficients control the overall process and are nearly the same whatever the tube material, so in gas-to-gas units the overall heat transfer coefficient of glass is typically within four percent of that of metal.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Glass-Tube Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: Corning has about 30 such heat recovery units on stream in Europe and five in the U.S., typically on spray drying exhausts in the food, dairy and chemical industries, for example cheese whey processing in dairies, and claims energy savings of up to 30 percent. Because glass, stainless steel and silicone elastomers all resist low-temperature corrosion strongly, the systems suit dirty, moist or corrosive gases and can run below the acid and water dewpoint temperatures with minimum difficulty. Cleaning is done online or off-line as the customer prefers; in the dairy industry two hours of each 24-hr day are typically spent cleaning, using automatic sprays of hot water, acid, or both. Gas-side fouling has not been a major problem in these applications, and payback is typically two to three years, in some cases as little as 6 months. Other energy intensive industries, such as steel or glass manufacturing, could use glass-tube exchangers at intermediate temperatures if ceramic seal technology is perfected, and Corning is also working with the Gas Appliance Technology Center on appliances where low-temperature fouling and corrosion are potential problems.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Corrosion-Resistant Low-Finned Tubes
paragraphs.text: Another design option is the low-finned tube, with external integral fins typically 19 - 30 fins/in., fin heights of 0.030 - 0.040 in., and a finned-to-plain-tube area ratio of about two to three. Such tubes have long been made in copper (Reference 3-43) and are now also made in carbon steel and several stainless steels and superalloys (Reference 3-44), though they have not yet been critically tested in fouling and corrosion service. In one current application, gases from burned coal are scrubbed by a flue gas desulfurization (FGD) process to remove sulfur oxides and particulate matter; scrubbing cools the gases and saturates them with water vapor, so they must be reheated before leaving the stack, commonly with steam-or-water-heated tube bundles. FGD interest has so far centered on the electric utilities but will grow in non-utility industries as coal use increases.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Corrosion-Resistant Low-Finned Tubes
paragraphs.text: Inline reheat systems place an inline tube bundle in the gas duct downstream of a mist eliminator, heated by steam or hot water, with tubes usually of carbon steel, Corten, Types 304, 316, 316L and 317L stainless steel, Hastelloy G, Inconel 625, or combinations. These systems have suffered both gas-side fouling and corrosion, sometimes so severe that even these alloys were unsatisfactory, and some installations with high-finned tubes of 3 fins/in found them fouling or plugging more than bare tube bundles (Reference 3-45). To overcome these difficulties, a FGD system with steam heating inside integral low-finned tubes was recently installed at the Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) in Wheatfield, Indiana (Reference 3-46). The tubes, made by High Performance Tube, Inc., Union, New Jersey, are Inconel 625 with 30 fins/in., 0.75-in. OD, 0.012-in. fin thickness, 0.032-in. fin height and a finned-to-plain-tube area ratio of 2.65, arranged on an inline layout with air-driven sootblowers.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Corrosion-Resistant Low-Finned Tubes
paragraphs.text: The NIPSCO unit came on stream in April 1983 and has been up and down since because of various boiler-related problems, but the reheat system, sootblowing included, appears to work properly; its long-term behavior in the severe fouling and corrosion environment is yet to be seen (References 3-47, 3-48). The low-finned exchanger is expected to perform well because (a) the same reheat can be done with about half the number of plain tubes, (b) fewer tube rows allow better sootblower cleaning, and (c) fewer tuberows reduce crossflow pressure drop relative to plain tubes. Success here could promote high performance low-finned tubes in place of plain tubes in other applications facing gas-side fouling and corrosion.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.1 Low-Temperature Range, T_gas < 500 F / Economizer Preheat System
paragraphs.text: Current engineering practice is often to keep heat exchanger surfaces hot enough to avoid cold-end corrosion, and for boiler economizers a common method is to preheat the feedwater so the economizer surface stays above the acid dewpoint temperature at all times. Kentube [Dyer (Reference 3-38)], which designs and builds economizers for industrial boilers, includes a feedwater preheat system in its standard economizer design, normally a shell-and-tube heat exchanger in which boiler steam preheats the feedwater. A temperature control valve regulates the steam flow to suit a range of low- and high-sulfur fuels. Lowering the economizer inlet feedwater temperature, as low-sulfur fuels allow, widens the steam-to-water temperature difference and so increases heat transfer, while raising it increases the safety margin against cold-end corrosion. With this auxiliary heat exchanger the designer can avoid economizer cold-end corrosion completely.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.2 Intermediate-Temperature Range, 500 F < T_gas < 1000 F / Coal-Fired Boilers
paragraphs.text: Several important heat-exchanger applications with potential fouling and corrosion problems lie in this range; coal-fired boilers are perhaps the most important, and two further examples are also given. Bryers (Reference 1-5) points out that liquid deposits on coal-fired steam generator surfaces can be highly corrosive, and all such liquid attack seen so far has involved alkali and sulfur compounds. The temperature ranges of accelerated corrosion correspond to the melting temperatures of these compounds, about 550 to 900 F. In a reducing atmosphere corrosion may be attributed to the pyrosulfates Na_2S_2O_7 and K_2S_2O_7. The iron-alkali trisulfates Na_3Fe(SO_4)_3 and K_3Fe(SO_4)_3 are mainly responsible for severe metal loss in superheaters and reheaters at metal temperatures of 1100 to 1300 F; opinions differ on whether the Fe_2O_3 in the trisulfate comes from coal ash or from tube scale, and hence on the exact tube wastage mechanism. The third and highest range (T_gas > 1500 F) involves sodium and potassium sulfates, highly corrosive when molten, but this alkali sulfate corrosion has not troubled most boiler heat-transfer equipment because steam generator metal parts never reach that temperature (Reference 1-5). Carbon steels resist scaling in combustion atmospheres up to about 1000 F but may oxidize faster at somewhat lower temperatures under high stress, so carbon steel superheater tubing is restricted to moderate temperatures and stainless steels and superalloys are used for more severe conditions.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.2 Intermediate-Temperature Range, 500 F < T_gas < 1000 F / Low-Sulfur-Content Corrosion
paragraphs.text: For heat recovery units in fired-heater operations, the main concern of Meith (Reference 3-33) is sulfur corrosion in exhaust gases from low sulfur fuels (less than one percent by volume as H_2S) at intermediate temperatures (500 - 700 F), which has been a major problem with carbon steel exchangers. ENTEC therefore uses this design procedure: a "muffler steel" containing 11 percent chromium in finned-tube bundles, with the first two or three rows made of plain tubes to shield the finned tubes. Meith firmly holds that thicker fins do not solve the corrosion problem and recommends that no fin exceed 0.050 in.; if corrosion calls for a thicker fin, the material should be changed instead. Grove (Reference 3-49), by contrast, recommends fins as thick as possible, for three reasons: thicker fins cost only nominally more, they resist erosion and corrosion better, and greater fin thickness raises fin efficiency and therefore heat transfer.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.2 Intermediate-Temperature Range, 500 F < T_gas < 1000 F / Low-Sulfur-Content Corrosion
paragraphs.text: Battelle Columbus Laboratories (BCL) has long studied gas-side fouling and corrosion from incinerating municipal solid wastes; its latest reported work dealt with burning a refuse and sewage sludge mixture in a municipal incinerator in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (Reference 3-50). The refuse included paper, wood, grass, garden waste, cloth, garbage, plastics, dirt, glass, ceramics and some metals, and the sludge averaged 3.4 percent sulfur and 0.09 percent chlorine. Exposure time, metal temperature and gas temperature were varied. Main results: (a) in 8-hr exposures, the corrosiveness of the refuse combustion environment to carbon steel was only half as great with sewage sludge present, with less reduction for Alloy T22, very little for Incoloy 825 and essentially none for Types 310 and 347 stainless steel; (b) corrosion resistance to the refuse-sludge mix, in decreasing order, was Incoloy 825, Type 310 stainless steel, Type 347 stainless steel, Type T22 stainless steel and Type A106 carbon steel, and an aluminized coating on steel stayed intact and could be a cost-effective alternative; (c) with sewage sludge, corrosion rates fell with exposure time and appeared to level off at about 1000 hours; (d) between 500 - 900 F metal temperature, corrosion rates rose with temperature for carbon and low alloy steels but fell for stainless steels; (e) short-term rates at gas temperatures of 1100 - 1200 F were only 1/5 of those at 1500 F and rose less with metal temperature. Throughout the BCL program, the overriding factor was chloride attack, which can be quite severe under both oxidizing and reducing conditions.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / Ceramic Heat Exchanger Development
paragraphs.text: The high-temperature regime involves extremely hostile exhaust gases; the topics here are ceramic heat exchanger development and the effect of gas-side fouling and corrosion on materials for high-temperature heat recovery in the aluminum and glass industries. The Gas Research Institute (GRI), Chicago, Illinois, is running a 3-year study to develop a ceramic recuperator and burner system recovering waste heat from several high-temperature industrial furnace exhausts at gas temperatures up to 2500 F. A closely related ceramic heat exchanger effort, the high temperature burner-duct-recuperator heat exchanger development (HTBDR) program, is sponsored by the DOE Office of Industrial Programs, and AiResearch Manufacturing Company, Torrance, California, is prime contractor for both (Reference 3-51).

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / Ceramic Heat Exchanger Development
paragraphs.text: GRI's main objectives are to design, develop, fabricate, field-test and establish the commercial feasibility of an advanced high-temperature ceramic recuperator and a high temperature combustion air burner (Reference 3-52); the burner is to run with combustion air preheat up to 2000 F on either gas or No. 2 fuel oil. A detailed design of a 5 MM Btu/hr prototype recuperator has been finished. It pairs a tubular ceramic heat exchanger in series with an AiResearch metallic plate-fin heat exchanger. The ceramic unit is a 2-pass tubular exchanger with flue gas flowing over the outside of tubes arranged on a 1.5-in. equilateral layout; the ceramic tubes are 48 in. long with inside and outside diameters of 0.75 and 1.00 in.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / Ceramic Heat Exchanger Development
paragraphs.text: One preliminary fouling-related task examined how candidate materials tolerate typical industrial flue gases, to help select the shell-and-tube materials for the prototype recuperator to be tested. The materials were sintered α-SiC, siliconized SiC, Si_3N_4-bonded SiC, recrystallized SiC and chemical vapor-deposited SiC. Tube samples were immersed in exhaust streams from a steel soaking pit, a steel forge furnace, an aluminum remelt furnace and a steel reheat furnace, at flue gas temperatures up to 2425 F for up to 185 days. Except in the aluminum remelt furnace exhaust, which left a glassy coating on the samples, the materials seemed to survive these environments in reasonably good condition. The tests were isothermal, however, and more critical tests of fouling effects during actual heat recovery are to follow.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Corrosion Response of Materials for High-Temperature Heat Recovery in the Aluminum Industry
paragraphs.text: GRI is also actively pursuing high-temperature heat recovery in the aluminum industry (Reference 3-51). Natural gas and Diesel fuel are the most widely used fuels, but aluminum remelt furnace exhaust also carries impurities from additives to the melt. The most severe environment in remelting is above the remelting pots, where halide fluxes remove surface oxides and chlorine gas is used for alloy sparging. A typical flux contains potassium and sodium chloride as a low melting material (1100 - 1200 F) that dissolves the fluoride salts, which are the active agents for oxide removal. The GRI program has concentrated on this area.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Corrosion Response of Materials for High-Temperature Heat Recovery in the Aluminum Industry
paragraphs.text: Solar Turbines Incorporated (Reference 3-53) recently finished a GRI study analyzing corrosion of 21 stainless steels, superalloys and ceramics in this aluminum remelt furnace environment. A 60-in. high test chamber was attached to the side of the exhaust stack of a remelt furnace, and test probes of 0.75-in. diameter for metals and 1.00-in. diameter for ceramics, each two to three feet long and mostly combining four materials, were exposed in it (materials in Table 3-2). The stack temperature was nominally 2000 F maximum, and the uncooled ceramic samples were tested at that temperature. The stainless steels and superalloys were air cooled to nominal maximum surface temperatures of 1200, 1500 F and 1500, 1700 F as shown in Table 3-2, except INCO 800, tested at 1000 F. Test durations ranged from 315 hr to 2448 hr.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Corrosion Response of Materials for High-Temperature Heat Recovery in the Aluminum Industry
paragraphs.text: All metal-alloy candidates (1200 - 1700 F) and SiC ceramic candidates ([판독 불가: symbol before] 2000 F) showed very high rates of tubewall recession, and none of the material designs showed reliably viable intrinsic protection at the test temperatures. The agents responsible are believed to be alkali-metal halides entrained in the recuperator flue gases; these molten halides foul tube surfaces and oxidize to the potent secondary reactants HCl and Cl_2, and analogous, equally reactive fluorine-containing compounds may also form. On all metal alloys these gases quickly consume the major constituents (Fe, Ni, Cr), first forming molten chloride mixtures and then voluminous oxides, and equally severe sulfidation-type attack was found on the nickel-base alloys Incoloy 825 and Hastelloy S. On SiC ceramics the same HCl and Cl_2 (and analogous HF + F_2) are thought to produce very volatile SiCl_4 and SiF_4 vapors, which consume the silicon-base matrices and binders and also weaken the remaining surface structure by disrupting SiX/Si^X and other inter-particle bonds; subsequent surface cracking and spalling of the weakened SiC contribute materially to the high recession rates.
