paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Impact of High-Temperature Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion in Glass Plants
paragraphs.text: Most glass plants recover heat from the 2800 F melting furnace exhaust with brick checkers-type periodic flow regenerators; these gases are extremely corrosive and have a tremendous gas-side fouling potential. Webb and Kulkarni (Reference 1-14) reviewed the fouling and corrosion problems in the top and bottom parts of the regenerator. Top Zone of Regenerator (2550 - 1830 F): (a) the high temperature gas flow erodes the bricks, and particulate carry over from the furnace (Na_2O, SiO_2, Al_2O_3, V_2O_5, CaO and cullet dust) settles in the packings with the eroded brick and partly blocks flow; (b) MgO in magnesite bricks reacts with SiO_2 from the exhaust to form forsterite (Mg_2SiO_4), causing volume expansion and then crumbling of the bricks; (c) aluminosilicate bricks used in earlier regenerators can be attacked by K_2CO_3 and Na_2SO_4, and SO_3 can convert CaO to CaSO_4 at temperatures as high as 2370 F, weakening the bricks; (d) vanadium oxide, V_2O_5, mainly from fuel oil, and Na_2SO_4 in the flue gas attack refractory bonding material, both accelerate SO_3 conversion of MgO and CaO to sulfates, and vanadium also fluxes the silica, leaving a liquid phase between MgO grains and lowering the brick melting temperature until the bricks start to crumble.

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Impact of High-Temperature Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion in Glass Plants
paragraphs.text: Bottom Zone of Regenerator (1830 F - 1100 F), item (a): sodium sulfate (Na_2SO_4), formed from Na_2O and SO_x gases, is liquid above 1625 F and partly deposits on the bricks. Liquid Na_2SO_4 is not corrosive in itself, but it dissolves SO_3 into a dilute solution and carries the SO_3 activity from the gas phase through the molten sulfate to the refractory surface. SO_3 continues to attack MgO in magnesite bricks, forming MgSO_4, and CaO in the silicate bond of these bricks is converted to CaSO_4; both reactions weaken the bricks: MgO + SO_3 --> MgSO_4; CaO + SO_3 --> CaSO_4 (magnesium oxide and calcium oxide in the brick react with sulfur trioxide to give magnesium sulfate and calcium sulfate).

paragraphs.section: 3.3.3 High-Temperature Range, T_gas > 1500 F / The Impact of High-Temperature Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion in Glass Plants
paragraphs.text: Bottom zone, continued: (b) the MgSO_4 and CaSO_4 formed this way dissolve in liquid Na_2SO_4 to give a ternary eutectic around 1200 F, which drips down the bricks and probably solidifies as white slag when the gas flow is reversed. (c) Na_2SO_4 that does not deposit on the bricks as liquid condenses as a white fluffy powder in the gas stream below its condensing point of 1623 F; together with white slag dripping from the hotter zone, these particulates plug passages in the bottom part of the regenerator packing, and once several passages are blocked the furnace must be shut down and the deposits removed by hand. (d) Alkali iron trisulfates may also form by reaction of Na_2SO_4, K_2SO_4 and Fe_2O_3 deposits, and sodium vanadates by reaction of Na_2SO_4 and V_2O_5 present in the exhaust; these sodium trisulfates and vanadates are corrosive.

Designing heat-transfer equipment for gas-side fouling service involves many variables. First, gas-side fouling factors are widely used to oversurface heat exchangers, but they are only a partial solution, since cleaning devices generally also have to be specified when dirty fuels are burned. Second, the designer can choose among many exchanger types for this service: recuperators, regenerators, direct contact exchangers, heat pipe exchangers and fluidized bed exchangers. Conventional recuperators, such as firetube boilers, watertube boilers, shell-and-tube, gas-to-air and finned-tube exchangers, have existed for many years and permit only relatively minor design changes, so innovative types such as direct contact and fluidized bed exchangers clearly need to be developed to overcome gas-side fouling. Third, materials are central. The most pressing materials problems lie (a) in low-temperature heat recovery, where acid condensation is a major problem and plastic, glass, coatings and alloy steel are possible solutions, and (b) in high-temperature applications, where development of superalloys and especially ceramic materials is essential.

Published gas-side fouling data are scarce, so most heat exchangers are sized with rule-of-thumb gas-side fouling factors (fouling resistances) drawn from experience rather than from measurements. Section 4 reviews whatever gas-side fouling data exist, lists values where suitable, compares the factors where possible and sums up the state of the art, using both the open literature and input from the industrial contacts named in the section.

The gas-side values span from 0.0005 hr-ft^2-F/Btu for natural gas up to 0.05 for coal, and the table groups flue gases as clean, average and dirty. For dirty gases, the recommended fouling factors make the exchanger oversurfaced, but this added surface presumes that cleaning devices will be fitted and operated on the unit.

paragraphs.section: 4.4 EG&G Idaho Diesel Exhaust Fouling Factors
paragraphs.text: Henslee and Bogue (Reference 4-5) ran experiments on gas-side fouling of a finned-tube heat exchanger placed in the exhaust of a stationary Diesel engine burning No. 2 Diesel fuel. Operating ranges were gas velocity 10 - 30 ft/sec, inlet gas temperature 350 - 580 F and outlet gas temperature 220 - 430 F. Runs 1, 2 and 3 lasted 300, 320 and 430 hours. The work followed an earlier AiResearch Manufacturing Company study (Reference 3-13) that used No. 6 fuel oil. Transient fouling resistances, shown in Fig. 4-1, peaked at about 0.14 hr-ft^2-F/Btu, and fouling became asymptotic after roughly 200 - 300 hours. The asymptotic deposit thickness with No. 2 Diesel fuel turned out to be essentially equal to that AiResearch found with No. 6 fuel oil, even though deposition rates differed. Henslee and Bogue tabulated all of their fouling data in their report; the authors regard this as the most complete gas-side fouling data set in the literature at the time, though too large to reproduce here.

paragraphs.section: 4.6 Air-Cooler Fouling Factor Used by Amoco Production Company
paragraphs.text: Amoco Production Company mainly produces natural gas, and the steam condensers at its facilities are mostly finned-tube air coolers. Amoco designers apply an air-side fouling factor of 0.003 hr-ft^2-F/Btu (Reference 4-8); this experience-based value covers both corrosion of the finned air-side surfaces and any dirt that collects on them.

paragraphs.section: 4.7 ENTEC Fired Heater and Waste Heat Boiler Fouling Factor
paragraphs.text: ENTEC (Reference 3-33) designs its fired heaters and heat recovery units with a fouling factor of 0.005 to 0.008 hr-ft^2-F/Btu. The range is largely independent of the particular contaminants in the combustion gas because ENTEC installs enough sootblowers to hold the fouling factor inside this band during normal operation (the ENTEC cleaning approach is discussed further in Section 6.4).

Important process-contaminated streams, such as those in the cement, aluminum and pulp and paper industries, are absent since no gas-side fouling factors exist for them.

paragraphs.text: The Henslee-Bogue values (Reference 4-5) are the only known experimental asymptotic gas-side fouling factors in the literature. Rogalski's gas turbine data (References 4-6, 4-7) are also experimental, but his tests clearly did not reach asymptotic conditions. All other entries are experience-based design values, probably somewhat lower than the expected asymptotic values, and in some cases (as Table 4-1 shows) cleaning devices are needed to keep fouling within the stated range. The Weierman, Zink (Reference 4-2) and Henslee-Bogue entries apply to finned tubes, Rogalski's probe was a smooth circular cylinder, and the TEMA values most likely refer to smooth surfaces though the TEMA tables (Reference 4-3) do not say so. The Zink values are additionally minimum recommended factors for the given service.

Three conclusions follow from Section 4: (a) few gas-side fouling factors are available in the literature and most rest on experience, not experiments; (b) where factors exist, the sources sometimes disagree noticeably; (c) for many applications, such as the cement, aluminum and pulp and paper industries, no gas-side fouling factors exist at all. These points echo a high-priority recommendation of the Gas-Side Fouling Workshop in Boulder, Colorado in October 1981 (Reference 1-11), whose 41 mostly industrial participants called for experimental gas-side fouling factors for typical industrial gas streams and typical exchanger geometries. Two years later that need was judged to be as pressing as ever.

paragraphs.section: 5 Startup and Shutdown Procedures to Minimize the Effects of Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Exchangers in gas-side fouling service are usually designed for a particular steady-state operating point, yet during startup, shutdown and off-design operation they run under other conditions. Section 5 looks at techniques used to limit gas-side fouling under these off-design conditions.

paragraphs.section: 5.1 Use of Clean Fuel during Startup Conditions
paragraphs.text: Several industrial contacts (References 5-1, 5-2) cite starting up on a clean fuel as common practice; a unit designed to burn residual oil, for instance, would likely be started on natural gas. Combustion conditions during startup matter greatly, and procedures have been devised to limit deposition from poor combustion; Watts (Reference 5-1) strongly recommended the Babcock and Wilcox procedures (Reference 3-22), on which much of this discussion draws. Bringing a cold boiler or other exchanger into service calls for low firing rates over a fairly long time to avoid expansion problems and possible overheating of superheaters or reheaters. Combustion efficiency is poor in this period, and with heavier oils, coal and other dirty fuels much unburned material can escape, so natural gas, with its low ignition temperature, is an ideal startup fuel.

paragraphs.section: 5.1 Use of Clean Fuel during Startup Conditions
paragraphs.text: Starting on fuel oil or coal carries hazards. After roughly an hour of firing, low pressure boilers can take load and high pressure boilers, usually fitted with air preheaters, begin delivering preheated air to the burners, aiding combustion; by then, however, the air preheater and economizer surfaces will have collected considerable oil or oily soot deposits. Such deposits ignite fairly easily and the resulting fire is hard to put out, and Theoclitus (Reference 5-3) has documented several such problems. One way to lower the fire risk is to blow sootblowers continuously on regenerative-type air preheaters as they rotate through the flue gas.

paragraphs.section: 5.1 Use of Clean Fuel during Startup Conditions
paragraphs.text: When oil has to be used for startup, Babcock and Wilcox (Reference 3-22) ranks firing methods as follows: (a) the safest method with the cleanest stack uses steam atomizers burning light fuel oil, No. 1 or No. 2, atomized with steam or compressed air; (b) next is steam atomization with oil no heavier than No. 6, heated as needed for proper atomization; (c) third is steam atomizer nozzles using compressed air for atomization with oil no heavier than No. 6, heated as needed; (d) starting on oil with mechanical atomizers is not recommended because of the oil and soot deposited in economizers and air preheaters and the associated fire hazard, especially in air preheaters. Stationary boilers that use mechanical atomizers for oil firing at 20 to 100 percent of maximum load are generally started on gas or with methods a, b or c on oil.

paragraphs.section: 5.2 Maintain Heat-Exchanger Surfaces above Dew-Point Temperatures
paragraphs.text: Frequent shutdowns and startups can lead to severe gas-side fouling and corrosion. One countermeasure is to keep exchanger surfaces above the acid and water dewpoints with hot air or another warm fluid (References 5-4, 5-5); this is expensive but may be justified in some applications given the consequences, and it also shortens the subsequent startup because the unit is already partly warm. AiResearch Manufacturing Company plate fin heat exchangers (Section 3) were used at a clay drying plant in California where startup was troublesome because condensables in the particulate-laden gas condensed on cold exchanger surfaces; heating the exchanger gradually and bringing it on stream essentially at operating conditions solved the problem (Reference 3-17). This case confirms that cold surfaces should not meet condensable-bearing gases during startup.

paragraphs.section: 5.3 Use of Bypass to Avoid Low Flow Velocities
paragraphs.text: As noted in Section 3, some fire-tube boilers have an internal or external bypass for controlling exit temperature in processes such as sulfuric acid production by sulfur burning. Although meant for exit gas temperature control, the bypass can also regulate exchanger velocities during startup and shutdown. Because the exchanger is sized for a given steady-state fouling factor, operating it clean requires a lower velocity; careful use of the temperature control bypass can reduce time spent at low velocities, where lower fluid shear stresses increase the tendency to foul.

paragraphs.section: 5.4 Experience with an Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycle System
paragraphs.text: Sundstrand Corporation built an Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycle (ORBC) system, used in several industrial and utility installations, intended for exhaust gas at 600 to 1000 F with toluene as working fluid. Units have been tested on Diesel engine exhausts and at a ceramics plant using exhaust from a ceramic drying kiln (References 5-6, 5-7, 5-8, 5-9). The Easton, Maryland public utility installation met several notable startup and shutdown problems. There the ORBC ran on the exhaust of two Diesel engines burning No. 2 Diesel fuel with about 0.2 percent by weight sulfur, for which the sulfuric acid dewpoint was calculated as 249 F. The engines ran only when generating was cheaper than buying grid power, so the unit typically operated about eight hours per day. The heat-transfer train comprised a boiler, a superheater and a preheater; the main gas-side fouling and corrosion occurred in the carbon steel preheater, whose welded carbon steel fins had a density of five fins per inch, thickness 0.050 in. and height 0.75 in.

paragraphs.section: 5.4 Experience with an Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycle System
paragraphs.text: After about six months of intermittent service the preheater cold end was heavily fouled while its hottest part had little fouling, so exhaust gas left at about 450 F instead of the 300 F design value, and the preheater pressure drop had risen to 6.78 in. H_2O against a design point of 3.89 in. (Figure 5-1, which gives the full cleaning history). First cleaning attempts, baking the unit dry at 750 F and injecting low temperature soot release chemicals, removed the mostly soot deposits and brought the bundle pressure drop to 5.8 in. H_2O, but much scale from corrosion products stayed. Oakite 32 with a steam lance was tried next without success. Finally Oakley Cleaning, a commercial firm, used Oakite 32, inhibited HCl and water to clean the exchanger almost completely, cutting the pressure drop to roughly 4 in. H_2O. In later operation, periodic baking plus low temperature soot release chemicals kept the preheater clean enough.

paragraphs.section: 5.4 Experience with an Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycle System
paragraphs.text: Two main contributors to the fouling and corrosion deposits were identified. Each daily startup began cold, with metal temperatures below the sulfuric acid dewpoint, so much acid condensed; a typical startup spent about 20 minutes below the acid dewpoint, and the acid badly attacked the fins at the preheater cold end. In addition, the exhaust stack was uncapped and uninsulated, so acid condensed inside it, ran down and attacked the last row of preheater tubes. Further measures listed in the report: the diverter valve was replaced by two valves in series with a fan pressurizing the space between them so that any leakage into the engine exhaust was ambient air, not engine gas; ORBC control settings were changed to shorten startup; and the number of startups and shutdowns was kept as low as possible. Each of these steps helped to some degree in reducing gas-side fouling and corrosion at this site.

Boilers normally have to be removed from service periodically for internal inspection, cleaning and repair. External cleaning of heat-transfer surfaces should be done as thoroughly as possible before the fire goes out and completed with air lances and scrapers after cooldown (Reference 3-22); deposits left in place at shutdown soak up acid and water condensate like a sponge and expose the surface to corrosion. Hung (Reference 5-10) described a notable shutdown practice from tests with a small firetube boiler assessing a waste heat boiler for an existing incinerator burning various pumpable and non-pumpable wastes, whose exhaust contained HCl and other corrosive species. Tests ran intermittently, typically 8 hr in the day with shutdown overnight, and every shutdown involved opening an inlet access door before switching off the fan so that ambient air purged HCl gas from the tubes before metal temperatures fell below the acid dewpoint. This limited acid condensation, and the tests showed carbon steel tubes could serve here if this and some other operating precautions were followed. Hung based the procedure on practices he had seen at full-scale incinerators.

Startups and shutdowns can cause serious gas-side fouling and corrosion because units then run away from their design conditions. The procedures reviewed in Section 5 are rather limited and some depend strongly on the site. New systems such as the Sundstrand Organic Rankine Bottoming Cycle are particularly exposed to these problems during installation and initial operation, and suitable operating procedures often have to be worked out by trial and error. Additional startup and shutdown procedures would therefore be very welcome to those dealing with gas-side fouling and corrosion.

paragraphs.section: 6 Gas-Side Fouling Prevention, Mitigation, and Accommodation Techniques
paragraphs.text: Industry deals with gas-side fouling through various prevention, mitigation and accommodation techniques, grouped here as fuel cleaning, control of combustion conditions, fuel and gas additives, surface cleaning, quenching, control of operating conditions and gas cleaning. Section 6 covers each, concentrating on additives, surface cleaning and control of operating conditions.

Ash and constituents such as sodium, sulfur and vanadium are wholly or partly responsible for deposits formed on heat-transfer surfaces by the gas-side fouling transport processes, so removing them before combustion is very desirable. Reference 3-22 states that processes exist to desulfurize and de-ash residual fuel oils. Water washing of residual oils has worked in some marine uses but will probably not spread widely since it removes only sodium and sediment; water washing out of service, and partly in service, has eased some problems with current fuel oils. Essenhigh (Reference 6-1) notes that commercial and experimental mechanical/physical coal cleaning methods such as gravity separation and froth flotation exist, but these remove only mineral matter, hence only inorganic sulfur, and do poorly on very fine, micron sized mineral particles. Chemical coal cleaning was still conceptual or experimental.

Thompson (Reference 3-27) stresses that controlling combustion to limit particulate formation in exhaust gas is central to preventing gas-side fouling and corrosion. Fuel type, combustion equipment and burner design all affect formation of particulates including soot; for example, well-distributed water droplets in a liquid fuel can greatly improve combustion and cut soot. The effect of different fuels' ash on downstream combustion gases is often poorly known. Thompson also names fuel injection pattern, fuel injection schedule and fuel viscosity control as important, and air preheaters are routinely used to raise combustion efficiency. Fuel variability causes difficulties: coal supplied to industrial users varies much more than utility coal, and agricultural or miscellaneous waste fuels can vary enough to drive downstream fouling. For the classic low-temperature H_2SO_4 condensation problem, one remedy is limiting excess air, which governs conversion of SO_2 to SO_3 and thus H_2SO_4 formation. Upstream combustion conditions therefore strongly influence downstream gas-side fouling and corrosion.

Premixing of air and fuel supports this view. White (Reference 6-2) examined how premixing JP-5 fuel and oxidizer affected gas-side fouling downstream of a gas turbine and found that fuel-air premixing practically eliminated soot, making it practically impossible to foul the downstream heat exchanger under those conditions; his observations are shown qualitatively in Figure 6-1. Figure 6-1: probable soot deposition rates as a function of combustion system parameters (Reference 6-2).

In some conditions chemical additives can raise combustion efficiency, lower emissions and lessen gas-side fouling and corrosion. Many proprietary additives are sold, with widely varying success, and Radway (Reference 6-3) observes that past sellers of cure-all "snake oil" formulations have bred skepticism, so that firms taking an open, scientific approach are often wrongly dismissed before presenting their evidence. The section treats additives for oil- and coal-fired systems separately, then presents a successful oil-fired boiler case and briefly explains why magnesium-based additives work.

Libutti (Reference 6-4) reported cold-end additive tests with No. 6 oil containing 0.9 - 2.5 percent sulfur in three utility and two industrial boilers, injecting powdered additives between the economizer and the air preheater. Calcium hydroxide, magnesium oxide, sodium aluminate, sodium carbonate, ammonium bicarbonate, activated alumina, expanded vermiculite and silica were tried at surface temperatures from 180 to 360 F. His conclusions: cold-end additives must have fine particle size; high absorptivity and at least moderate alkalinity are desirable; and aluminum oxide, ammonium bicarbonate, magnesium oxide and silica are suitable powdered cold-end additive constituents.

Battelle Columbus Laboratories (BCL), sponsored by the Electric Power Research Institute, documented the state of the art on additives for coal and oil firing through a 1980 literature review (Reference 1-9) and a workshop later that year (Reference 1-10); though aimed at utilities, the findings apply to similar industrial conditions. For residual oils, three elements cause fouling that additives can relieve: sulfur, vanadium and sodium. Some sodium is natural in crude oil, but most in residual oil comes from seawater contamination during shipping, and refinery desalting leaves about 10 - 30 ppm. On combustion most sulfur becomes SO_2, about one percent of which converts to SO_3, which combines with water vapor to give H_2SO_4; iron and vanadium compounds can catalyze further SO_2-to-SO_3 conversion through the boiler. Vanadium oxidizes to V_2O_5, which may react with sodium and other trace metals to form metal vanadates. Table 6-1 (from Reference 1-10) lists additives effective for SO_3-related problems, including low-temperature corrosion and fouling, chiefly MgO, Mg(OH)_2, Mg metal, Mg-Mn and dolomite; Table 6-2 lists additives effective for vanadium- and sodium-related high-temperature fouling and corrosion, again mainly Mg-based and Mn additives.

The workshop concluded on additives for residual oil fouling and corrosion (Reference 1-10) that MgO in oil dispersion is the most effective additive against vanadium and sulfur trioxide corrosion, that many other additives can help depending on circumstances, that additive performance is site specific so results from one boiler do not carry over directly to another, and that many questions remain, including how best to run test programs. Later, Krause et al. (Reference 6-5) tested magnesium- and manganese-based additives in residual fuel oils and found: low excess air alone cut flue gas SO_3 as well as MgO and MnO additives at high excess air; combining low excess air with additives sharply reduced SO_3 and minimized deposits; magnesium or manganese additives substantially lowered deposit adherence for a low Na/V ratio fuel; fine particle (2 microns or less) MgO best reduced high-temperature corrosion, with manganese oxide giving some reduction; and aluminum or silicon used with MgO neither lowered deposit adherence with a high-sodium, high-vanadium fuel nor helped corrosion rates of the exposed alloys.

The Battelle survey and workshop showed far less additive work for coal-fired systems than for residual oils. As Table 6-3 shows, MgO/Oil, MgO + Mn/Dry, CaCO_3 and boron-based additives have been tried against high-temperature fouling and for ash modification, but only boron-based additives have significant experience, and only for ash modification. The workshop's general conclusions on coal additives (Reference 1-10) were that additives developed for oil firing sometimes help but are neither optimal nor adequate in all cases, and that better data are needed on slag behavior, deposit effects, corrosion suppression, plume-visibility reduction and coal handling. Radway (Reference 6-3) concedes that how tiny amounts of dispersed magnesium prevent or remove boiler deposits is not fully understood, and Thompson (Reference 3-27) likewise sees a strong need for carefully controlled additive experiments to understand the basic phenomena and why some additives succeed and others fail.

paragraphs.section: 6.3.3 Oil-Fired Additives: A Brief Case History
paragraphs.text: Cold-end gas-side fouling and corrosion arises when flue gas SO_3 condenses as H_2SO_4 on the cooler ends of air preheaters and other exchangers. South Carolina Electric and Gas Company (SCE&G) had cold-end corrosion in two Ljungstrom air preheaters on an oil-fired utility boiler (Reference 6-5). Of three options considered (raise exit gas temperature, reduce SO_3 concentration, or lower O_2 to reduce SO_2-to-SO_3 conversion), only reducing SO_3 was judged practical, which could be done by lowering oxygen in the combustion air, switching to lower-sulfur fuel, or neutralizing gaseous SO_3 with chemical additives. The No. 6 oil had 2.1 - 2.2 percent sulfur, 0.082 percent ash and 360 ppm vanadium, and the high vanadium, a catalyst for SO_2-to-SO_3 conversion, was a definite problem. On technical and economic grounds SCE&G chose chemical treatment with the Coaltrol M Flue Gas Neutralizing System, a proprietary powder injected into the duct upstream of the air preheaters. Soon after, inspection showed the preheaters in better condition with less plugging. SO_3 fell 93 percent, from 30.7 ppm to 2.2 ppm, and the acid dewpoint from 289 F to 252 F, so besides reducing fouling and corrosion the regenerators could run at a lower exit gas temperature, saving about $100,000 per year in energy against a one-time feed system capital cost of $80,000.

paragraphs.section: 6.3.4 The Mitigating Effects of Magnesium-Based Additives
paragraphs.text: As the case history showed, additives can sometimes lower SO_3 in combustion gases, which lowers the acid dewpoint and the quantity of H_2SO_4 condensing on cool surfaces. Alkaline earths such as magnesium can also be beneficial in combustion gases that contain sodium. Na_2O + SO_3 --> Na_2SO_4 (6-1) (formation of sodium sulfate, whose deposition is common in the cement, glass, pulp and paper and most other industries). 3Na_2SO_4 + Fe_2O_3 + 3SO_3 --> 2Na_3Fe(SO_4)_3 (6-2) (Na_2SO_4 deposits react with gas-stream SO_3 and iron oxide to form sodium-iron trisulfate, a tenacious, corrosive deposit). MgO + SO_3 --> MgSO_4 (6-3) (magnesium oxide captures SO_3 as magnesium sulfate, whose deposits are softer and more friable than Na_2SO_4 and so easier to remove). 2MgSO_4 + Na_2SO_4 --> Na_2Mg(SO_4)_3 (6-4) (magnesium sulfate reacts with sodium sulfate to give sodium-magnesium trisulfate, also softer and more friable than sodium-iron trisulfate). Because MgO reacts more readily with SO_3 than Na does, reaction 6-3 is favored over 6-1. These reactions give some basis for the success of Mg-based additives, but many questions about additive effectiveness are unresolved, and although work so far has centered on MgO, further study may yield other additives.

Industry has developed and used several surface cleaning techniques, including steam and air sootblowing, sonic sootblowing and water washing, with chemical, mechanical and thermal cleaning used to some extent; each is covered in this section.

Steam or air sootblowing is the most common way to clean gas-side fouled heat-transfer surfaces, and Table 6-4 outlines sootblower design and operating parameters (Reference 3-22). The blowing medium is usually air or dry steam, and its pressure and temperature matter. Sootblower location and spacing within the exchanger are very important, as are nozzle number, type, size and angle of attack. Blowing speed and frequency depend at least on fuel type, excess air and operating conditions. Table 6-4. Sootblower Design and Operation (Reference 3-22): 1.
