Rotary and Retractable Sootblowers. DiCarlo (Reference 6-7) described the two main sootblower types, rotary and long retractable (Figure 6-2). A rotary sootblower has a multi-nozzle element fixed permanently in the tube bank, with one nozzle per tube lane. A long retractable sootblower can be run manually or automatically, with blowing pressure adjustable at the head from 100 - 350 psig. Since rotary blowers are always exposed to flue gas, they are limited to gas temperatures below 1000 F, whereas long retractables can serve at almost any gas temperature. Figure 6-2: the rotary and long retractable sootblowers (Reference 6-7).

Sootblower Specification as a Function of Ash Content. ENTEC designs, builds and installs fired heaters and waste heat boilers and, thanks to its approach, finds gas-side fouling not serious (Reference 3-33): the steam sootblower type is chosen according to fuel ash content (Table 6-5). Specifying sootblower number and type this way keeps the gas-side fouling factor at 0.005 - 0.008 hr-ft^2-F/Btu in operation. At that fouling level the gas-side heat transfer coefficient, not the gas-side fouling resistance, controls; the bigger concern is tubeside fouling resistance, which the large outside-to-inside area ratio from external fins magnifies. Table 6-5. ENTEC Sootblower Specification as a Function of Ash Content (Reference 3-33): ash content < 0.08 percent: No Problem; 0.08 to 0.12: Stationary; 0.12 to 0.2: Rotary; > 0.2: Traversing.

Frequency of Sootblowing. Because sootblowing costs money, its frequency matters. Formerly one blow per shift, three per 24-hr day, was standard in many boiler plants; optimum cleaning cycles are still not precisely known, but some plants now use more refined methods. At the St. Regis Paper Plant, which fires black liquor in recovery boilers, steam sootblowers start when bundle pressure drop reaches a preset value (Reference 6-8), and Young (Reference 6-8) reports that a rise in outlet gas temperature, reflecting deposits impeding heat transfer, can serve the same purpose. A computer-control system installed at the Rauma-Repola Oy Pulp Mill in Finland, which burns spent sulfite liquor (Reference 6-10), must remove deposits including Na_2CO_3, Na_2SO_4, Na_2S_2O_7 and NaHSO_4, some corrosive. Gas-side temperatures, heat transfer coefficients and pressure drops plus feedwater temperatures are sensed; the recovery boiler sootblowers form six individually controlled groups, and when a parameter tied to a group passes its preset value the computer fires that group, so blowing happens only when and where needed. Sootblowing steam use dropped from 4.8 to 3.0 percent of total plant steam generation, and the boiler stayed cleaner than before.

Both low- and high-frequency sound have been tried for cleaning fouled surfaces, but attention has centered on low-frequency horns. KVB, Inc., Irvine, California, began selling Swedish-made sonic sootblowers (sonic horns) about 6 or 7 years earlier (References 6-11, 6-12, 6-13); about 600 operate in the U.S. and 1000 worldwide, in precipitators, recovery boiler hoppers, direct-fired boilers, heat recovery boilers, CO boilers, air preheaters and process heaters. Forty-five U.S. installations are on heat-transfer equipment handling combustion gas from oil, wastes, bark, black liquor, coal, residual oil, NH_4B sulfite [as printed], wood, red liquor and refuse; installations in the current year include a waste heat boiler on miscellaneous wastes, an economizer on a black liquor recovery boiler in pulp and paper, a coal-burning electric utility and a waste heat boiler in a refinery acid decomposition process. The KVB Acousticlean Sonic Sootblower (Figure 6-3) runs at 220 Hz, sounding much like a ship's horn; it is 24 in. long, 12 in. maximum diameter and weighs 65 lb, using 60 to 80 psi air at 40 - 80 SCFM per horn. The horn is typically stainless steel and the diaphragm, the only moving part, titanium or stainless steel, allowing use in gas up to 1900 F; effective cleaning needs at least 130 decibels (db). Sound-wave vibration energy fluidizes soot and other attached particles by breaking their bonds to each other and the surface, after which they fall away under gravity or gas stream forces. Figure 6-3: the KVB Acousticlean Sonic Sootblower (Reference 6-11).

Horn effectiveness is usually judged by monitoring the exchanger outlet temperature, which then sets the cleaning cycle. Diamond Power Specialty Company, Lancaster, Ohio, makes and sells a low frequency sonic sootblower under agreement with Mats Olson Konsult AB of Sweden: the Diamond Power Infrasonic Hz-20, operating at an inaudible 20 Hz at 130 - 135 db (schematic in Figure 6-4, Reference 6-14). It is just over 15 ft long, weighs 650 lb, has a carbon steel resonance tube and diaphragm, and needs at least 75 psig air at 200 - 700 SCFM depending on application. Applications include boilers, economizers and air preheaters. On a large finned tube recovery boiler economizer about 20 ft by 6.5 ft by 40 ft high, which previously needed a continuously running shot system, the horn running six minutes every half hour (20 percent of the time) kept the unit operable and was estimated to save $34,000 per year in maintenance, capital and operating costs. On a 110 tons of steam per hour boiler with plain tubes firing No. 5 and 6 fuel oil, which had six steam sootblowers used four times per day (two retractables between the secondary and primary superheaters, two retractables between the primary superheater and the first economizer bank, two rotaries between the first and second economizer tube banks), an Infrasonic Hz-20 was put between the secondary and primary superheaters, and none of the steam sootblowers has had to run since. Figure 6-4: the Diamond Power Infrasonic Hz-20 Sonic Sootblower (Reference 6-14).

General observations on sonic horns: they work best on light, fluffy deposits and lose effectiveness as deposits become sticky and tenacious. Their cleaning cycle differs markedly from steam sootblowers, which typically blow once per shift, whereas horns sound more or less continuously. Horns cost more to buy than steam sootblowers but much less to operate (Reference 6-11). Most horns have been retrofitted to exchangers not designed for them, indicating they are generally added only when a plant has serious gas-side fouling, essentially as a last resort. Sticky deposits have defeated horns in some cases, yet many horns are operating successfully.

Water washing is common for air preheaters and other heat-transfer equipment, and water soluble deposits come off readily if enough water is used. The standard washer is a stationary, high-penetration, multi-nozzle device whose high velocity jets remove deposits through high fluid shear stress together with thermal shock contractions; most of this discussion follows Reference 6-15. For air preheaters, washers are normally placed at both hot and cold ends and run together, with nozzle number and orifice diameter depending on exchanger size. Fresh water is normally used, and a saltwater wash should be followed by a fresh water rinse. Rivers, lakes and ponds are the usual sources, with well water and house-service water also widely used; the water must be free of debris that could plug exchanger passages or clog nozzles and pumps.

Washing frequency depends on fuel quality, deposit type and amount, operating conditions, dryness of any sootblowing medium and other factors. Washing can be done (a) out-of-service, (b) in-service isolated or (c) in-service on-stream. Out-of-service washing happens during scheduled shutdowns for inspection, maintenance or repair and allows the closest control and thorough inspection of the surface before, during and after washing; all deposits must be fully removed, because leftover residue can bake onto the surface and become extremely hard to remove. In-service isolated washing cleans one exchanger of a two-or-more exchanger installation by reducing boiler load and isolating it with dampers and fan shutdown while the boiler stays on line and the other unit keeps running. On-stream washing is done with gas and the other fluid still flowing, and suits only installations whose ductwork and drain locations prevent or minimize moisture reaching dust collectors, precipitators, wind boxes and boilers. When insoluble material carried from the boiler lodges as large particles in hot-end flow passages, standard washers struggle, so special high-energy jet equipment using intermediate pressure (400 - 1000 psig) and high volume (600 - 1200 gal/min) has been developed.

Remaining cleaning methods fall into chemical, mechanical and thermal categories. Chemical cleaning of gas-side deposits is usually done off-line. Thermal cleaning, also called self-cleaning or baking at elevated temperature, heats the exchanger and holds it hot until deposits bake off; Shah (Reference 3-19) reported its use for plate-fin exchangers in the paint and pulp and paper industries, where modular units let fouled modules be swapped for clean ones and cleaned thermally off-line. Mechanical cleaning suits gas-side deposits better and includes shot, surface vibration, mechanical brushing and scouring with nutshells. Metal brushes and nutshells were mentioned in Section 3 for a fluidized bed exchanger and an FCCU exhaust heat recovery system. Shot cleaning drops small metal or ceramic shot over the top of the exchanger; it scours the surface while falling by gravity, is gathered at the bottom, carried back to the top and reused as needed, in some cases continuously (Reference 6-14).

Shaking or vibrating a tube bundle is sometimes used (Reference 3-1) in the primary metals industry, where copper or zinc ores and pyrites are roasted in a fluidized bed to break down the ore into a material fit for reduction. Roasting yields a dusty SO_2-bearing gas used to make H_2SO_4, which is cooled from about 1800 to 750 F before gas cleanup. The very dusty gas calls for a modified boiler design, for instance a vertical platen exchanger with gas outside the tube bank. Dust and metal particles stick to the tubes and need frequent removal, but steam sootblowing is unwanted because it alters gas composition and adds moisture, so shaking or vibrating the bundle works very well. Conseco (Reference 6-16) developed a water-tube heat-recovery boiler cleaned by vibration, with a vibratory vertical grid heat-transfer surface rated for particle loadings up to 30 grains/ft^3, offered with plain or finned tubes and a modular design permitting single-tube replacement without disturbing the others. Built from various corrosion-resistant materials, it has served on off gas from an incinerator burning sewage cake treated with ferric chloride.

paragraphs.section: 6.4.5 Cleaning Techniques for Plate-Fin Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: AiResearch carried out extensive cleaning tests on its plate-fin heat exchangers (Reference 3-17) to assess their use in glass-melting furnace exhaust as part of a Brayton cycle heat recovery system. Aims were to (a) evaluate gas-side fouling of several plate-fin configurations, (b) develop effective cleaning methods and (c) determine fouling linked to several gas-stream constituents. Two cleaning methods were developed: (a) an air lance with movable high-pressure air jets blowing in the hot-gas flow direction, and (b) an air cannon releasing a sudden large volume of high pressure (150 psig) air against the hot gas flow.

paragraphs.section: 6.4.5 Cleaning Techniques for Plate-Fin Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: In the first test series (Reference 6-17), dust from working glass furnaces plus suitable gaseous species were injected into natural gas combustion products to simulate the exhaust, entering at about 1250 F with velocities of 19 to 31 ft/sec. Five plate-fin modules with 3 - 7.5 fins/in., plain and offset fins, were tested with hot-end and cold-end fouling observed. Hot-end dust deposits were light and fluffy and easily blown off. Offset fins fouled about 8 to 10 times faster than plain fins; the air lance cleaned plain-fin cores on line but not offset fins, and the air cannon, which also needed a temporary shutdown, did poorly on offset fins too, so offset-fin cores were judged unsuitable where gas-side fouling may occur. At the cold end, condensing H_2SO_4 and water badly corroded Type 409 stainless steel, ruling it out, and the mixed condensate-flue dust deposit resisted both air cannon and air lance, requiring off-line cleaning with steam or water injection.

paragraphs.section: 6.4.5 Cleaning Techniques for Plate-Fin Heat Exchangers
paragraphs.text: The second series (Reference 6-18) used 1450 F inlet gas and 24 ft/sec face velocity with a Type 409 stainless steel core of 7.5 plain fins per inch, this time holding cold-end temperatures above the acid and water dewpoints. Sodium sulfate in the dust combined with gas-stream SO_3 to form sodium pyrosulfate, given in the report as Na_2SO_4 + SO_4 --> Na_2S_2O_7 (6-5) (sodium sulfate plus sulfur oxide yielding sodium pyrosulfate; the second reactant is printed as SO_4 although the text refers to SO_3), and Na_2S_2O_7 tended to deposit on cold-end surfaces. Hot-end deposits were again light, fluffy and removable with the air lance, but at the cold end Na_2S_2O_7 acted as a "glue" capturing more particulates; the air lance failed when Na_2S_2O_7 exceeded about 10 percent of the deposit but worked for smaller fractions. Deposit pH tracked the Na_2S_2O_7 fraction and hence cleanability: above a pH of about three the cold end could be air-lanced. Keeping the coldest corner of the crossflow exchanger above roughly 400 F in these tests let the air lance prevent fouling, and in accompanying corrosion tests Type 310 stainless steel performed best. As an alternative to raising cold-end metal temperature, adding MgO to neutralize SO_3 and so limit Na_2S_2O_7 formation was suggested. The work shows the value of knowing deposit constituents and their forming reactions and matching the cleaning method to the deposit, and the finding that offset-fin surfaces foul more readily is useful design knowledge.

Quenching lowers the temperature of a hot flue gas so that molten and soft particles solidify and do not stick to cooler heat transfer surfaces. Four quench fluids are used (Reference 5-1): (a) cool flue gases, (b) steam, (c) air and (d) water spray; cool flue gas quench is probably the most and water spray the least desirable. A cement industry case (Reference 3-9) shows how well quenching works when done correctly.

Cementos Mexicanos planned a four-stage preheater kiln at its Torreon Plant, and raw-material analysis indicated an alkali by-pass of up to 7.5 percent would be needed to avoid preheater buildups. The by-pass removes 7.5 percent of kiln exit gas bearing alkali-chloride vapors before they condense on the colder preheater feed. The extracted gas at 1920 F is quenched at once with 77 F air to a mix gas temperature of about 710 F to freeze the alkali salts quickly. Because the gas was to be cleaned in a glass bag dust collector, secondary cooling to 530 F before the collector was needed. Two options were compared: Alternate A added 7300 SCFM of 77 F dilution air to cool 13,400 SCFM of mix gas from 710 to 480 F, requiring a dust collector and ID fan sized for 20,700 SCFM at 480 F; Alternate B cooled the 13,400 SCFM indirectly in a gas cooling heat exchanger, shrinking the dust collector, ID fan and motor by 35 percent. The savings on these items far exceeded the exchanger cost, so Alternate B had lower capital and operating costs, though there was concern that alkali salts would condense on the cool exchanger walls.

Cementos Mexicanos concluded after careful evaluation that quenching kiln exit gas rapidly from 1920 F to 710 F would turn the alkali salts from liquid to solid before they reached the exchanger tubes, preventing wall buildups, and installed a Smith Gas Cooling Heat Exchanger to cool 13,400 SCFM from 710 to 480 F at 0.6 in. water pressure drop. In operation since September 1980, it has a single continuously running 20-hp fan, with a thermocouple at the dust collector inlet setting the dilution air damper to hold 480 F. Periodic inspection shows clean tube inside walls, and the tubes have never needed cleaning nor the unit any maintenance.

Properly controlled operating conditions are a key way to lessen gas-side fouling, the classic example being keeping surface temperatures above the acid dewpoint at the cold end of low-temperature heat recovery systems. The section describes what two industrial firms do and two examples showing why controlled conditions matter. Monsanto Chemical Operations: Monsanto Chemical Intermediates Company's Chocolate Bayou Plant in Alvin, Texas (Reference 3-32) makes several intermediate chemicals, chiefly acrylonitrile, plus others including a poultry food supplement, and uses furnaces for steam generation, process applications and waste incineration. Of the incinerator feedstocks, only phenol process bottoms containing sodium sulfate salts caused trouble: the waste-heat boiler fouled from Na_2SO_4 deposition. Steam soot blowers once per shift control it, and problems arise if this is not applied consistently; done properly, the unit runs four to six months between cleaning shutdowns, triggered by a preset rise in stack temperature. Input Na_2SO_4 concentration is about one percent, as required to meet stack particulate emission limits. A softball-size deposit chunk showed clear signs of amorphous Na_2SO_4 formed from the liquid state, yet no corrosion has been seen.

Bethlehem Steel Heat Recovery: Bethlehem Steel uses compact recuperators on box annealing furnaces (Reference 6-19), brazed stainless steel plate-fin units made by Garrett AiResearch Manufacturing Company in a partly DOE-sponsored program, rated at 1500 F. The furnace gas, coke oven off-gas with 50 grains/100 SCF of particulate, preheats air to 1200 - 1300 F, and flue gas leaves the recuperator at 180 - 230 F, in the acid dewpoint range. The unit corroded and plugged; owing to counterflow the cold zone moved deeper into the unit, and after six months it was about one-third plugged. Stalactites formed at the hot end, composed of iron (from the furnace) and chromium and nickel (from braze alloys and the exchanger), while cold-end deposits held iron, chromium, nickel and sulfur. Units cycle every two to three days with about one-half day down; one unit/burner is installed and all hot surfaces are clean. Owing to pre-installation concern about dewpoint corrosion, coupons with braze material were tested and showed no corrosion. After about one year of operation, with Battelle Columbus analyzing data, fuel savings are estimated at about 23 percent (baseline 0.925 MM Btu/ton versus 0.716 MM Btu/ton with the recuperator), though eliminating acid dewpoint problems is expected to cost two to three percent of those savings; as a rule of thumb, a 50 F lower air temperature costs about one percent in fuel savings. Bethlehem Steel expects increasing use of by-product gases such as coke oven gas in steelmaking.

Diesel Exhaust Fouling: AiResearch (Reference 3-13) studied gas-side fouling downstream of a Diesel engine burning No. 6 Diesel fuel at length, placing a finned-tube module in the engine exhaust to observe fouling and corrosion under real operation; such controlled tests can give very useful insight into fouling and corrosion in full-scale industrial exchangers. Main findings reported by DeAnda (Reference 3-13): (a) running the module below the acid dewpoint in No. 6 Diesel fuel exhaust caused no corrosion despite H_2SO_4 being present; (b) between 150 and 550 F two fouling mechanisms occurred, acid condensation and hydrocarbon condensation: a thin acid film condenses first, soot particles stick to the wet surface and absorb the H_2SO_4, and as rising fouling resistance raises the deposit surface temperature above the acid dewpoint, acid condensation stops and further buildup is from unburned hydrocarbons; (c) uncooled surfaces showed no deposition; (d) fin type did not affect fouling rate, plain- and segmented-finned tubes with equal fin density and height fouling alike; (e) fouling rose with more fins per unit length; (f) pressure drop climbed quickly over the first 48 hours, matching a rapid fall in heat transfer performance.

Switch Condenser: in one chemical industry application (Reference 3-39) deposition from the gas is actually wanted and depends on tightly controlled conditions. Phthalic anhydride is a key intermediate for dyes such as eosin, rhodamines, erythrosin, quinoline yellow, copper phthalocyanine and phenolphthalein, and for making anthraquinone and its derivatives. It is produced by controlled oxidation of ortho-xylene or naphthalene over a V_2O_5 catalyst in a tubular reactor; the product gases pass over a finned tube bundle cooled internally by chilled water, depositing the phthalic anhydride (sublimation temperature 130.8 F) on the surface. When a sensor detects that bundle pressure drop has passed a critical value, the tubeside fluid is switched from water to a heating medium slightly hotter than the phthalic anhydride melting point, hence the name switch condenser; the product melts off the fins into a receiving vessel, after which the fluid is switched back to water and the cycle repeats.

Particulates can be removed from gases with electrostatic precipitators, mechanical collectors, fabric filters and wet scrubbers; gaseous pollutants are harder to remove with standard methods such as limestone addition, wet scrubbing without sulfur recovery, MgO systems with sulfur recovery and dry sorbent systems (Reference 3-22). Mostly such removal is done for environmental reasons and usually downstream of the heat exchanger, but three techniques applicable to heat-transfer equipment are discussed. Amoco Production Company's main product is natural gas, and its furnaces and heat recovery units see practically no gas-side fouling because the fuel is very clean: the gas goes through molecular sieves to strip entrained organic liquid droplets, water wash and other sweetening steps to remove sulfur, and alumina beds for drying. The deposits observed seem to be sand drawn into the furnace with combustion air (Reference 4-8).

Harwell Laboratory in the United Kingdom has studied ceramic fabric filters for removing particulates from heavy-fuel Diesel exhaust. The filters are woven ceramic fiber of 95 percent Al_2O_3 and five percent SiO_2; exhaust entered the outer part of an annulus, passed through the filter and left through the center tube, with several bags in parallel to ease cleaning. Effective filtration needed a light filter cake, formed when 0.3 micron particles plugged the filter, and an hourly reverse air pulse shed the accumulated particles. Pressure drop through the system ranged from 1.18 to 9.45 in. H_2O; the maximum is a severe constraint because the engine tolerates very little back pressure. For 0.5 micron average particles collection efficiency was 82 - 95 percent. The technique works but is prohibitively expensive; where exhaust must be cleaned for environmental reasons anyway, it should perform well and lower particulate fouling potential as a bonus (Reference 6-20).

From laboratory tests of a firetube boiler in waste incinerator exhaust, Hung (Reference 5-10) concluded that placing a cyclone ahead of a waste heat boiler in heavily particulate-laden flue gas would clearly help: it would keep large, heavy particles out of the boiler and add retention time for complete oxidation if incinerator temperature surged suddenly, for example when waste composition changes, and more complete oxidation would also reduce unburned soot deposition on boiler tubes. Sotter (Reference 3-35) notes that in a boiler, dirty particulate-laden combustion gas typically contacts surfaces serving three functions: (a) heat transfer for direct-fired heating or heat recovery, (b) scrubbers and similar devices removing unwanted gaseous components such as SO_2, and (c) devices such as electrostatic precipitators removing particulates. He stressed the strong economic and operating incentives to merge these into one operation for a more efficient, cheaper process, an area needing innovative ideas.

Section 6 reviewed gas-side fouling prevention, mitigation and accommodation techniques. Fuel and gas cleaning have had limited success. Controlling combustion, though hard especially with variable fuels, affects particulate and impurity levels in exhaust and is very important. Fuel and gas additives have drawn much attention, MgO being the most widely used, but more work is needed, particularly for coal and non-oil fuels, including carefully controlled experiments to learn why some additives work and others do not and to develop new ones. Surface cleaning is probably the most important topic, being one of industry's most effective tools against gas-side fouling: steam and air sootblowing are mature and widespread, and recent interest in optimum cleaning cycles, including computer control, should make it cheaper and more efficient. Sonic sootblowers (horns) have seen growing U.S. use over the last five years as non-intrusive cleaning, mostly as retrofits; they are very effective on soft, friable deposits but poor on wet, sticky ones, and their successful operating limits need better definition. Water washing is widespread with fairly standard procedures, and mechanical methods such as shot and nutshell scouring are often effective. Quenching, rapid cooling of hot gas, is sometimes used to solidify particulates that would otherwise deposit on cooled surfaces. Finally, controlling operating conditions such as gas and surface temperatures is very important for minimizing deposits from dirty gases.

Putting a cost on gas-side fouling in industry is very hard. Some aspects are generic, but specific problems differ between industries owing to different fuels, processes and operating conditions, and even within one industry the cost factors are highly uncertain, so the few economic analyses done so far carry large uncertainty. The basic cost contributors are nonetheless well established: (a) increased capital costs, (b) increased maintenance costs, (c) loss of production and (d) energy losses. Each is discussed, followed by several quantitative cost analyses drawn from publications and personal contacts made during the study.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 The Deleterious Effects of Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Higher capital costs come partly from oversizing equipment for expected fouling. First, the low thermal conductivity of the fouling layer adds thermal resistance, demanding more surface for a given duty, and because gas-side fouling factors are poorly known, overly large safety factors can make designs very conservative. Second, the fouling layer narrows flow passages and raises pressure drop, requiring larger, more powerful fans; in some cases this capital increase equals or exceeds that from oversurfacing. Third, where on-stream cleaning is needed, the cleaning equipment itself adds capital cost.

paragraphs.section: 7.1 The Deleterious Effects of Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Maintenance costs are dominated by cleaning and additives. Waste heat boilers are usually cleaned with steam or air sootblowers; sonic devices look promising especially for light, fluffy deposits, and water washing is another key method (Section 6). Cleaning is done on-stream wherever possible, but if fouling forces a shutdown, manual cleaning adds maintenance cost, as is routine for suspension preheaters in the cement industry. Troubleshooting fouling and the associated chemical and other analyses add further cost. Additives attract much interest but can be expensive: in 1979 oil soluble MgO additive products cost $4.00 to $8.00 per pound (Radway et al., Reference 7-1).

paragraphs.section: 7.1 The Deleterious Effects of Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Production loss can be very large depending on the problem: deposits in any of the exchangers of Section 3 can cause downtime or reduced-capacity operation, and beyond product lost during downtime, extra time is usually needed for cooling down at shutdown and heating up at startup. Though hard to quantify, it is clearly important. Energy losses include the obvious reduced heat transfer and higher fan power from larger pressure drops, but more serious is that dirty gas streams are simply exhausted because heat recovery would risk fouling, maintenance and production losses. In the glass industry, for example, practically no heat is recovered downstream of brick checker regenerators for this reason (Reference 1-14), and flue gas at 1000 - 1200 F goes straight to atmosphere. Still, if recovered energy is not urgently needed it will not be used regardless of fouling. Much energy is also exhausted from U.S. cement plants (Reference 1-13).

paragraphs.section: 7.2 Thackery's Analysis of the Cost of Fouling in the United Kingdom
paragraphs.text: Very few attempts have been made to quantify fouling costs of any type because of the many uncertainties; Thackery (Reference 7-2) describes such estimates as a series of "considered guesses," yet his work is clearly the best and most thorough in this area. He estimated the cost of all fouling types in the United Kingdom, assigning a value in British pounds to each cost element, and arrived at 370-490 million pounds sterling (1978 values), covering both gas-side and liquid-side fouling; the breakdown is in Table 7-1. Table 7-1. Estimated Annual Costs of Fouling in the United Kingdom (Reference 7-2), estimated cost (1978): Capital Costs=£100 million; Maintenance Costs=70 - 90 million; Loss of Production=100 million; Energy Losses=100 - 200 million; Total=£370 - 490 million.

paragraphs.section: 7.3 Weierman's Analysis of Gas-Side Fouling Costs on Equipment
paragraphs.text: This analysis by R. C. Weierman of Escoa Fintube Corporation comes from Reference 7-3. Fossil fuels provide over 60 quadrillion Btu per year in the U.S., nearly 30 percent of it used directly for industrial heating, and they supply over 80 percent of industrial process energy, a dependence likely to last decades. Because energy is not always a large share of production cost even in energy intensive industries, industrial energy efficiency is often as low as 10 percent and rarely above 30 percent, so large savings are thought possible with existing, emerging and advanced technology. Better maintenance and operation and small equipment changes save some energy, but big savings need major process changes and capital. The best near-term prospect is recovering or using part of the 12 quadrillion Btu now exhausted to the environment, worth over $24 billion in fuel at about $2 per million Btu; 10-20 percent of it is thought economically recoverable in the near term if certain technical problems are solved.

paragraphs.section: 7.3 Weierman's Analysis of Gas-Side Fouling Costs on Equipment
paragraphs.text: Gas-side fouling of the recovery exchangers is one of the main technical obstacles; the high fouling potential of fossil fuel flue gas and the difficulty of cleaning usually raise equipment, maintenance and production costs. Two basic approaches exist: (a) change the process to reduce fouling, and (b) design equipment to work under the expected fouling. Process modification is the more sophisticated route but is generally long term, so adapting equipment designs is the most practical short-term path. If fouling were solved, about 2 quadrillion Btu, or $4 billion in fuel costs, per year would be recoverable with current or near-term technology. To make such equipment attractive, overdesign must drop and reliability rise; in some dirty applications fouling has almost doubled equipment cost, raising an average $15,000 per million Btu/hr transferred in clean service to about $25,000 per million Btu/hr in dirty gas. Recovering the 2 quadrillion Btu/yr would therefore need about $3 billion extra capital.

paragraphs.section: 7.3 Weierman's Analysis of Gas-Side Fouling Costs on Equipment
paragraphs.text: Weierman did not annualize these capital costs; taking an average 10-year life gives about $300 million per year in excess equipment capital due to gas-side fouling. He also assumed higher maintenance costs, estimating from "limited experience" annual maintenance at about 25 percent of original equipment cost versus about 10 percent in fairly clean service; with $7 billion initial equipment cost the fouling-related increase is about 15 percent, or $1 billion per year. The annual total is thus $0.3 billion capital plus $1 billion maintenance, $1.3 billion, which is below the $4 billion of Reference 7-3 because Weierman's added capital costs were not annualized.

Dyer (Reference 3-38) estimated steam sootblowing costs in U.S. industry. For a watertube steam boiler with steam at $5.33 per 100 lbm, allowing time to bleed the steam lines and a 1-3 minute blow per nozzle, each nozzle blowing costs $0.26 in steam. With four sootblowers of 15 nozzles each, run once per 8-hr shift on a 3-shift day, cleaning the boiler surface takes about $17,000 of steam over 365 days. Industrial steam generators may also have a superheater, economizer, air preheater and sometimes a reheater; Dyer assumed an average boiler has one exchanger besides the boiler surface, giving about $34,000 per year to sootblow a typical industrial boiler. The cheapest sootblower costs about $1,000 installed (Reference 7-4), so annualized capital is minor compared with operating cost. With about 50,000 industrial watertube boilers in the country (Chiogioji, Reference 2-1), U.S. annual steam sootblowing cost is about $1.7 billion. A 1980 KVB, Inc. analysis (Reference 7-5) of a typical industrial boiler with three steam sootblowers running 1.6 hours per day at a total 12,000 lbm/hr, with steam at $3.10 per 1000 lbm (1983-adjusted), gives $21,800 per year for one exchanger; despite differing steam flowrate, blow duration and steam cost, the KVB and Dyer estimates agree within 25 percent.

paragraphs.section: 7.5 Estimated Costs of Gas-Side Fouling in Cement Plants
paragraphs.text: Marner (Reference 1-13) estimated gas-side fouling costs for the U.S. cement industry. To value the unused energy in plant exhaust streams, each stream's temperature level and annual energy content were set, and a Rankine bottoming cycle with a steam or organic fluid boiler driving a turbine was assumed to convert it to electricity at an efficiency varying linearly from zero at 100 F to 35 percent at 1900 F, with a 40 percent maximum; pricing electricity at the 1982 U.S. industrial rate of $0.045 per kW-hr gave each stream a dollar value. Annual production loss, extra maintenance and capital costs due to fouling were also estimated, for a total of $238 million per year, surely a conservative figure (summarized in Table 7-2). Table 7-2. Summary of Estimated Annual Costs in U.S. Cement Plants Due to Gas-Side Fouling, Corrosion, and Erosion (Reference 1-13), estimated cost (1982 dollars): Capital Costs=$5 million; Maintenance Costs=4 million; Loss of Production=108 million; Energy Losses=121 million; Total=$238 million.

paragraphs.section: 7.6 Gas-Side Fouling Costs in the Petroleum Industry
paragraphs.text: The petroleum industry uses many kinds of heat-transfer equipment, such as furnaces with waste heat boilers and recuperators for cracking crude oil streams and ethylene processing. At Shell Oil Company, which burns fuel oil, gas-side fouling is a potential problem; per E. Barrington (Reference 5-2), Shell puts fouling energy losses at about $1 per barrel of oil burned, roughly three percent of fuel cost at about $30 per 42-gallon barrel. Extending this to the whole industry using the share of oil burned in non-feedstock uses such as process steam and direct heating, about 55 percent according to Chiogioji (Reference 2-1), gives about $92 million per year of gas-side fouling energy losses. Van Nostrand, Leach and Haluska (Reference 7-6) estimated liquid-side fouling energy losses of hydrocarbon streams in major refinery unit operations at $614 million (1983 dollars), so gas-side fouling adds about 15 percent on top of that.

paragraphs.section: 7.7 Total Gas-Side Fouling Costs in U.S. Industries
paragraphs.text: The section's data are combined into an annual U.S. total, with each assumption stated. Capital costs follow Thackery (Reference 7-2), who found gas-side equipment to be about 34 percent of the U.K. heat exchanger market; assuming the same U.S. share and a U.S.-to-U.K. Gross National Product (GNP) ratio of seven gives about $650 million per year of U.S. sales of gas-side fouling equipment, and Weierman's (Reference 7-3) estimate that 40 percent of capital cost is due to fouling yields $0.3 billion. Maintenance is based on Dyer's cleaning costs (Reference 3-38) plus 20 percent for cleaning other industrial heat-exchange equipment, giving $2.1 billion per year, possibly an overestimate since gains in heat transfer and pressure drop from cleaning are ignored. Energy losses are the petroleum industry's $92 million/yr (Section 7.6) scaled by the ratio of total energy use to petroleum industry use from Chiogioji (Reference 2-1), giving $0.9 billion/yr. Production losses, scaled from Thackery's values by the GNP ratio as for capital, are $0.3 billion/yr. The total is $3.6 billion per year (Table 7-3), led by maintenance at $2.1 billion/yr and energy losses at $0.9 billion; despite many assumptions this appears reasonable.

paragraphs.section: 7.7 Total Gas-Side Fouling Costs in U.S. Industries
paragraphs.text: Table 7-3. Estimated Annual Gas-Side Fouling Costs in U.S. Industries: Capital Costs=$0.3 billion; Maintenance Costs=2.1 billion; Loss of Production=0.3 billion; Energy Losses=0.9 billion; Total=$3.6 billion.

Difficulty in assessing fouling cost factors has kept economic analyses few, and those that exist often rest on doubtful assumptions; still, the available totals suggest gas-side fouling costs U.S. industry between $1 and $4 billion per year. Industry efforts to cut these costs vary and depend largely on how severe the problem is. The cement industry uses far less energy than the petroleum industry, yet its gas-side fouling energy losses, about $121 million/yr, exceed the petroleum industry's $92 million/yr, reflecting the more severe fouling from process-contaminated exhaust in cement plants. More accurate estimates require more statistics on the number of operating exchangers and fairly detailed data on gas-side fouling problems in each energy intensive industry.

paragraphs.section: 8 Additional Considerations Relating to Gas-Side Fouling
paragraphs.text: Section 8 briefly covers further topics: characterization of combustion gases, gas-side fouling measuring devices, fouling and corrosion from burning waste materials, and dissemination of gas-side fouling information.

Thompson (Reference 3-27), Young (Reference 6-8) and Anson (Reference 8-1) all stress characterizing combustion gas streams from a fouling standpoint, covering particle loading, composition and size distribution, gaseous components including excess air, dewpoints of the various gaseous constituents, and ash fusion temperatures. Characterization depends strongly on fuel composition, combustion conditions and any process contamination after combustion; downstream chemical reactions can also change gas composition, and gas temperature strongly affects particulate state and the transport processes during deposition. Thompson and others emphasize fuel composition in particular, and the ASME Research Committee on Corrosion and Deposits from Combustion Gases has tabulated twenty-six parameters, each with definition, purpose and expected measurement precision, for judging coal quality regarding furnace fouling and slagging (Reference 1-4).

Diesel engine exhausts are probably the best characterized combustion gases, chiefly through work by KVB, Inc. and Garrett AiResearch Manufacturing Company (References 8-2, 8-3). Surveys have covered exhaust gas characterization in the cement (Reference 1-13), glass (References 1-4, 8-4) and steel, aluminum and glass (Reference 8-5) industries, with the glass industry probably most studied at high temperature, but all these surveys found gaps, and many other industrial gas streams remain inadequately characterized. Anson (Reference 8-1) sums up the state of the art: a central issue is how the amount and nature of foulants relate to fuel type and combustion conditions; data are insufficient to define dirty industrial gas streams and how they vary with process conditions and fuels, especially above 1000 F, where corrosive interactions and chemical bonding are likely, and below 300 F, where large amounts of condensed phases may exist; and without such data neither heat transfer hardware nor fouling mitigation procedures can be properly designed or selected. A good understanding of gas characterization is needed to understand basic fouling mechanisms, and much more work is required.

The October 1981 Gas-Side Fouling Workshop in Boulder, Colorado (Reference 1-11) stressed the need for a standardized gas-side fouling probe. As a first step, a survey of fouling measuring devices, nearly complete (Reference 8-6), reviews about 25 devices and identifies five types: (a) heat flux meters, (b) mass accumulation probes, (c) optical devices, (d) deposition probes and (e) acid condensation probes. Heat flux meters track local heat flux to follow deposit buildup and so far have been used only in the radiation sections of boilers and fired heaters. Mass accumulation probes measure deposit mass quantitatively, while deposition probes collect deposits qualitatively. Optical devices use interferometry, ellipsometry and similar methods and are still confined to the laboratory. Acid condensation probes collect liquid acid below the acid dewpoint. Apart from Rogalski's heat-pipe device (References 4-6, 4-7), no probe yet can measure long-term online gas-side fouling resistances; the probes have yielded much useful information, but mostly on deposit analysis rather than fouling resistance, and gas characterization and deposit analysis are essential for interpreting probe results.

An ideal industrial probe would be simple, robust, lightweight, inexpensive and accurate, able to monitor online gas-side fouling resistances and to expose several materials at once for corrosion analysis, with reliable temperature control for tests at constant surface temperature; no probe yet meets all of these. Deposition probes have been used in pulp and paper recovery boilers, municipal incinerators and various oil- and coal-fired boilers, as well as in laboratory studies (Reference 8-6). Williams and Unmack (References 3-29, 3-30) are building a deposition probe for their fluidized bed work in the aluminum industry (Section 3), and Maberry (Reference 3-9), Bhatty (Reference 8-7) and Tresouthick (Reference 8-8) showed strong interest in using a probe to assess fouling and corrosion potential of cement industry exhaust streams; iron and steel, glass, copper, foodstuffs and textile industries are other candidates. The authors conclude that a gas-side fouling probe, probably cylindrical given that geometry's practical importance, should be designed, built and tested in several typical industrial exhaust streams to become a universally accepted tool, with a standardized way of collecting, analyzing and reporting data and continuing input from an industrial board to ensure it meets industry needs.

paragraphs.section: 8.3 Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion Problems Related to the Burning of Waste Materials
paragraphs.text: The U.S. produces huge amounts of waste each year. Agricultural wastes include sawdust, wood chips, hog fuel, rice hulls, nut shells, fruit pits and bagasse; miscellaneous (non-agricultural) wastes include garbage, plastics, dirt, metals, refuse, sewage sludge, waste liquids, chemical wastes, waste lube oil, waste solvents, used tires, shredded PVC and paint sludges. Heating values range from 3,860 Btu/lbm for oil sludge to 18,000 Btu/lbm for polyethylene residue (Reference 8-9). Industrial contacts (References 3-9, 3-27, 3-38, 5-1, 5-4, 6-9) showed strong interest in burning all kinds of waste, especially as landfills are no longer available in many regions. Burning wastes leaves very large amounts of energy in the gases leaving the thermal oxidizer or incinerator, but recovering it can bring very severe gas-side fouling and corrosion.

paragraphs.section: 8.3 Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion Problems Related to the Burning of Waste Materials
paragraphs.text: The pulp and paper industry has long burned hog fuel (wood product wastes in paper mills) and kraft and sulfite liquor in recovery boilers, not without difficulty; as noted in Section 3, such recovery boilers are especially prone to Na_2SO_4, Na_2CO_3 and NaCl deposits. Battelle Columbus Laboratories (Reference 3-50) has studied fouling and corrosion from incinerating refuse, sewage sludge, plastics, rubber and other solid wastes over the long term, finding chloride attack, which corrodes severely under both oxidizing and reducing conditions, to be the main issue, so materials selection for heat-transfer equipment is a key problem in waste disposal. Tresouthick (Reference 8-8) reviewed burning wastes such as waste lube oil, waste solvents, petroleum coke, wood chips, sawdust, chlorinated hydrocarbons, acid sludge, municipal refuse and shredded PVC in cement kilns. General Portland, Inc. burns wastes in two cement plants, at Paulding, Ohio and near Gorman, California (Reference 8-10), including 5 million gallons per year of spent solvents, paint residue, used cutting and lube oil and other materials; rotary kiln combustion reaches about 3000 F with 3.5 seconds residence time, destroying almost all the waste including chlorinated hydrocarbons. However, the company recently dropped its bid to burn wastes in kilns near Dallas, Texas because of local environmental concerns. Most waste-burning experience is in municipal incinerators and pulp and paper mills, but industrial incineration is expected to grow, and variable waste fuel composition plus severe downstream fouling and corrosion will be a formidable challenge.

The survey made clear that getting gas-side fouling information to industrial people is a problem: many contacts did not know of recent papers, reports, conferences and activities, and an even bigger issue is that many lack time to read and digest the literature even when they have it. The DOE-SERI "Workshop on the Research Needs of Heat Transfer Processes and Equipment" in Vail, Colorado, June 1981 (Reference 8-11), covering heat-transfer topics including fouling and corrosion, noted in its summaries that dissemination involves critical state-of-the-art reviews, bibliographies, organized literature retrieval and design methods; that the flood of new information must be systematically absorbed, categorized and made usable by designers, with major gaps remaining; and that fouling/corrosion/erosion is an area needing such efforts. Information dissemination was one of five of 21 items ranked high priority at that workshop.

For gas-side fouling, bibliographies such as the Fouling Prevention Research Digest from the United Kingdom (Reference 8-12) and professional development like the ASME Short Course "Fouling of Heat Transfer Equipment" (Reference 1-19) help but are not enough. Industrial contacts were very interested in the "Gas-Side Fouling Bibliography" presented at the 1983 ASME-JSME Thermal Engineering Joint Conference (Reference 1-17), which lists 206 references in a general category or one of four major categories, each further sub-categorized and cross-referenced against fuel type in two large tables so readers can quickly find a topic, the feature they liked most; since it covers only selected references since 1970, expanding and periodically updating it was suggested. There was also strong interest in Reference 1-18, an updated version of the 1970 Battelle Columbus bibliography with over 2000 references on ash deposits and corrosion grouped under key words, then in press for release that fall.

No easy solution exists. Many people who design, specify and make heat-transfer equipment, particularly in smaller firms, carry several major responsibilities and have little time for professional development, so condensing R&D results into concise, practical form is especially valuable. Employers should value professional development more and support employees attending meetings and conferences; professional societies should do more, for example the ASME Research Committee on Corrosion and Deposits from Combustion Gases and the ASME Heat Transfer Division K-10 Committee on Heat Transfer Equipment should publicize their work and look for ways to help; and DOE should revisit its publication policies and find new ways to get information to industry so it is used rather than left on a shelf.

Although considerable progress has been made on some gas-side fouling problems, many issues are unresolved. Section 9 lists high-priority gas-side fouling R&D needs as industry sees them, favoring generic projects over industry-specific ones. Industrial representatives agreed almost unanimously with the seven recommendations of the 1981 Gas-Side Fouling Workshop in Boulder, Colorado (Reference 1-11), which form the first seven entries of Table 9-1. Four further areas were identified: (a) fouling and corrosion from incinerating waste materials, (b) materials development for gas-side fouling service, (c) additives to mitigate gas-side fouling, and (d) dissemination of gas-side fouling information, giving 11 high-priority recommendations in all, each briefly explained using Reference 1-11 and earlier parts of the report.

Table 9-1. R&D Recommendations for Industrial Gas-Side Fouling: 1. Characterization of Combustion Gases; 2. Design, Development, and Testing of a Gas-Side Fouling Measuring Device; 3. Fundamental Studies of Attachment and Removal Mechanisms and the Development of Predictive Methods for Gas-Side Fouling; 4. Experimental Measurement of Gas-Side Fouling Factors for Specific Geometries; 5. Effectiveness of Cleaning Devices for Gas-Side Fouling Service; 6. A Comprehensive Study of the Fouling and Corrosion Mechanisms Associated with Acid Dewpoint Condensation; 7. Development of Alternative Types of Heat-Exchange Equipment to Mitigate the Effects of Gas-Side Fouling; 8. A Study of Gas-Side Fouling and Corrosion Problems Related to the Incineration of Waste Materials; 9. Development of Materials for Gas-Side Fouling Service; 10. A Fundamental Study of Additives to Mitigate the Effects of Gas-Side Fouling; 11. Dissemination of Gas-Side Fouling Information.

Characterizing combustion gases means determining gaseous components and particulate properties as functions of temperature; fuel composition, combustion conditions and post-combustion process contamination strongly affect it, and it is essential for understanding fouling transport processes. Diesel engine exhausts, and partly gas turbine exhausts, are reasonably well characterized, but most industrial streams are not, so the key industrial combustion gases, especially high-temperature streams in the aluminum, cement, copper, glass and steel industries, should be characterized. A gas-side fouling probe, probably cylindrical, should be designed, built and tested in several typical industrial gas streams; it should be simple, robust, lightweight, inexpensive, able to monitor online fouling resistances and test several materials at once for corrosion, with reliable temperature control, together with a standardized data collection, analysis and reporting method, developed with key industrial input to become a universally accepted tool.

Using the probe, fundamental studies of attachment and removal mechanisms should systematically vary gas composition, gas temperature, surface temperature, gas velocity and other key parameters, and once these mechanisms are quantitatively understood, predictive methods should be developed. Experimentally based design fouling factors hardly exist; apart from gas turbine and Diesel engine exhausts, most factors in use rest on experience, so transient gas-side fouling factors should be measured for specific geometries in typical gas streams as functions of those same parameters, possibly limited initially by scoping studies. The effectiveness of cleaning devices also needs systematic study of how well they remove typical deposits from common surfaces, covering air and water sootblowing, water washing, sonic sootblowing and selected mechanical and thermal techniques, to give designers guidelines for choosing the best cleaning for a given geometry and deposit.

Fouling and corrosion from acid dewpoint condensation is a major problem in low-temperature heat recovery, so a study should (a) measure transient gas-side fouling factors versus gas composition, gas temperature, surface temperature, gas velocity and other key parameters, and (b) identify accommodation techniques such as additives, materials selection including coatings, cleaning methods, and suitable shutdown, startup and transient operating conditions. Besides long-established recuperators and regenerators, alternative exchangers such as direct contact and fluidized bed heat exchangers have been developed to counter fouling and corrosion, and their continued development deserves high priority.

Given strong interest in incinerating agricultural and miscellaneous wastes, a study should determine fouling and corrosion characteristics of burning selected wastes, considering gas composition, gas temperature, gas velocity, surface geometry, surface material and fuel supply variation. Materials development is also very important: studies should find suitable materials and coatings for (a) low-temperature service with potential acid dewpoint condensation and (b) high-temperature service, where ceramics may be the only option, and stainless steels and superalloys should continue to be developed for intermediate-temperature service with corrosion problems. Magnesium-based additives are widely used with oil firing, but how they mitigate fouling is not fully understood, so a fundamental study should (a) clarify why additives succeed in some cases but not others and (b) develop new and better additives, testing residual oils, coal and emerging fuels such as coal-water mixtures.

Information dissemination matters because many who design, specify and build heat-transfer equipment have little time for it, so condensing R&D results into concise, usable form is especially helpful. There is no easy fix; bibliographies and reviews help, but much more is needed, and employers, employees, professional societies and DOE should all seek solutions, with DOE in particular revisiting its publication policies so that information reaches and is used by industry instead of gathering dust on a shelf.
